utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Today we are going to hear the closing arguments by Mr. Jokic's Defence. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. As planned, we are going to make our closing arguments today within about 200 minutes or so. That would be about three to three and a half hours. I hope that it may be even shorter. Your Honours, gentlemen of the Prosecution, we are nearing the end of this long and complex trial. After 145 trial days, after viva voce and 92 bis and 94 bis Prosecution witnesses, 93 of them, after hearing 42 witnesses that were brought before this Honourable Trial Chamber by the Defence of Mr. Blagojevic, and after hearing 14 witnesses that were called by the Defence of Dragan Jokic, and adducing about 1.000 exhibits on the part of all the participants in these proceedings, we are now to address you in accordance with Article 86 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. This Defence does not want this closing argument to be overextensive. We don't want it to be repetitive. We don't want to repeat what we've already said in the final brief. And bearing in mind all the elements of our defence which we did present in our final brief, today we wish to point out the key elements of this case which stem from the evidence adduced and the legal aspects of the indictment against Dragan Jokic. We would particularly like to refer to some of the things said in the closing arguments presented on Wednesday by Mr. Waespi of the Prosecution. Let us take things in order. In the last amended joinder indictment against the accused Vidoje Blagojevic and our client, Dragan Jokic, our client, Dragan Jokic, was charged that he participated as a member of the Zvornik Brigade in the period encompassed by the indictment and the crimes that were committed in the territory of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik. The position that Dragan Jokic had at the time was described in paragraphs 13 and 14 of the amended joinder indictment. According to these allegations, in July 1995, Dragan Jokic was a staff officer in the Zvornik Brigade, and he carried out the duties of chief of engineering. And as the indictment says, he was responsible for planning, directing, organising, and monitoring the activities of the Zvornik Brigade engineering company. And further on, they say that he was thus empowered to issue orders to the engineers company which implemented directives of the commander or the Chief of Staff of that same brigade. The second segment of this entire story, as it were, is paragraph 14 of the indictment where Dragan Jokic is charged that as duty officer at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade from the morning of the 14th of July, 1995, until the morning of the 15th of July, 1995, was charged with the duty of conveying orders from the higher command to subordinate units and, at the same time, he was tasked with drafting or sending reports to the higher command or to relay them. The indictment says what we've been dealing with about all these days, that the duty officer is the central point of coordination and communications for the Zvornik Brigade zone of responsibility. On the basis of such a position held by Dragan Jokic, the Prosecution concludes that he has individual criminal responsibility on the basis of Article 7(1) of the Statute in the commission, planning, instigation, aiding, and abetting, and supporting the preparations and perpetration of the crimes that occurred in the mentioned period in the territory of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik. This is described in paragraph 27 of the indictment. The Prosecution believes that Dragan Jokic, having held the position of operations duty officer and chief of engineering in the Zvornik Brigade was a member of the joint criminal enterprise because he could have foreseen - I underline the word "foreseen" because we will talk about it to a considerable degree - that the forces of the VRS and the MUP, during and after the joint criminal enterprise, will carry out opportunistic criminal acts such as those described in this indictment. Also that specifically as chief of engineering, he assisted in planning, monitoring, organising and carrying out the burials involved in the murder operation, while as operations officer, again he assisted in coordinating communication between VRS officers and commands involving the transport, detention, execution, and burial of the Srebrenica Muslims. In the factual basis of the indictment, this particular segment of the obligations that the chief of engineering had and that Dragan was charged with was described in paragraphs 46.4, 46.6, 46.8 through 46.12, and 51 of the indictment. As a member of the joint criminal enterprise, he has been charged with many opportunistic killings that took place in the territory of Bratunac and Zvornik. Your Honours, on the basis of such factual allegations made in the indictment, the Prosecution, both in the indictment and after the judgement related to 98 bis, the Prosecution comes to the conclusion that Dragan Jokic committed crimes from counts 2 to 5 of the indictment, namely described in Article 2 -- in count 2 of the indictment and punishable by Articles 5(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. You did hear that the Prosecution believes that they proved beyond reasonable doubt by adducing their own evidence that four elements were met which are otherwise required as proof of extermination as a crime against humanity. Number one, that there was an armed conflict, which we are not denying. Number two, that the actions taken by Dragan Jokic are associated with a widespread and systematic attack aimed against the civilian population caused the death of victims, and that the actions and omissions of Dragan Jokic were unlawful, either out of intent - we are going to refer to that - advertent recklessness, or gross negligence. And fourthly, that Dragan Jokic was within a broader context in which his conduct took place. Not to repeat myself, in paragraphs 3 and 4 of the indictment, the Prosecutor comes to the conclusion that Dragan Jokic, as a member of the joint criminal enterprise, also committed crimes of murder as a crime against humanity and violations of the laws and customs of war. And count 5 of the indictment states, and they tried to prove this through these proceedings, that Dragan Jokic also committed the crime of persecution as a crime against humanity, which is reflected in cruel and inhumane treatment, terrorising the civilian population, and destroying their personal property. In the briefest possible terms, acting in accordance with the powers derived from Rule 98 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, this Defence, on the 28th of February, 2004, and at the end of the Prosecution case, this Defence submitted to this Honourable Trial Chamber a motion for acquittal on all counts in respect of Dragan Jokic. Your Honours, in your judgement of the 5th of April, 2004, that is to say after the Prosecution case, you established that in respect of Dragan Jokic, on counts 2 to 5, in terms of his individual criminal responsibility under Article 7(1) of the Statute, he was acquitted of all these counts in the part that relates to planning, instigating and ordering the crimes. Also, in the same judgement, in relation to Dragan Jokic the Trial Chamber rejected the factual allegations contained in paragraph 45(b) and (e), 47.2, 47.5, except for the witness named Resid Sinanovic, and for paragraphs 47.7 and 47.8 of the indictment. What guided us in our work that followed when we presented our own case was your conclusion that no reasonable trier of fact could reach a finding beyond reasonable doubt that Dragan Jokic ordered the crimes of murder, extermination or persecution per se. Therefore, they removed these three heads of responsibility for all the crimes with which Dragan Jokic has been charged. However, the conclusion that a reasonable trier of facts could find, on the basis of the evidence adduced by the Prosecution, if it were to be accepted, could lead to the conclusion that Dragan Jokic was a member of the joint criminal enterprise and that he participated in the execution and aiding and abetting of these crimes by, I quote, "Knowingly provided assistance in the commission of crimes he is charged with and that he could, therefore, incur individual criminal responsibility as an aider and abettor." That is the core of what we wish to speak about, proceeding from res judicata. After this -- after this decision of the Trial Chamber, the Defence case of Mr. Blagojevic and Mr. Jokic followed, and in the opinion or, rather, in the modest opinion of this Defence, these two Defence cases led to a different conclusion on the position of the accused Dragan Jokic, his knowledge on the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, and the objectives of this enterprise, especially about his consciousness and intent, mens rea, in terms of assisting the perpetrators of these crimes through his own knowledge. In this closing argument, we will try to address precisely the results of the overall proceedings, not only an analysis of the Prosecution evidence. In order to prove that Dragan Jokic was a participant in joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecution must prove beyond any reasonable doubt all the criteria established in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. In order for someone to be convicted as a member of a joint criminal enterprise, it is necessary to meet many requirements. And with regard to this matter, the Honourable Trial Chamber and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal have already taken a position; namely, we have already heard all of this, that is, that participation in a joint criminal enterprise can be considered in one of the following ways: By direct participation in the commission of these crimes, and that there is agreement among the perpetrators of these crimes. Then, also, the accused could knowingly assist the perpetration of this crime or instigate another person to commit this same crime. And thirdly, if acting in a way which would assist a particular system within which this crime is perpetrated by virtue of the fact that he holds a particular position with certain powers and that he has knowledge about the nature of this system and the intent to support and promote this. According to paragraph 36 of the indictment and bearing in mind paragraph 77 of the judgement in accordance with Rule 98 bis, it appears that Dragan Jokic knowingly assisted the commission of the crimes that he has been charged with. Your Honours, on the basis of the evidence we heard, in order to reach such a conclusion and in order to have this conclusion be a well-argumented one, beyond any reasonable doubt, according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and which was dealt with, inter alia, in the appeals judgement in the Aleksovski case, it is necessary to meet several requirements. First of all, that the accused committed a crime which consists of practical assistance, instigation or moral support and which in turn would have a considerable influence on the commission of crimes by the main perpetrator. Secondly, it is necessary to establish that Dragan Jokic was aware of the main elements committed by the chief perpetrator. And the third and key question related to establishing affiliation with joint criminal enterprise as an aider and abettor is to prove mens rea, the mens rea required by an aider and abettor, and which means that an aider and abettor knows that his actions and activities do assist the commission of a certain crime on the part of the main perpetrator. Such jurisprudence of the Tribunal has been expressed in the appeals judgements in Krstic and Tadic, as well as the Kunarac judgement. However, Your Honours, while I was preparing my introduction today and listening to the Prosecutor's closing arguments, as well as their theory of a joint criminal enterprise, and while I was listening to Mr. Karnavas's closing argument yesterday, at one point it simply occurred to me that it would be a useless waste of time for me to use these closing arguments to further comment on this theory of joint criminal enterprise. You know this far better than I do. You can always go back to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal to check any of our positions against that background. However, I deem it necessary in view of Article 24 of the Statute of this Tribunal to draw your attention to the case law and jurisprudence of the country from which both my client and I come from, which certainly has a bearing when determining the kind and length of sentence to possibly be imposed. And we believe this is something that the Chamber should take into account. Please allow me to use this opportunity to say a couple of words about the legal framework that was in place at the time relevant to the indictment. In July 1995 in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also in the federation and in Republika Srpska, the same law applied that had been taken over from the former Social Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was no longer called the Criminal Code of the SFRY but, rather, the Criminal Code of Republika Srpska, general provisions. We changed the cover, but the book remained the same. In Article 24 of that law, the law that prevailed at the time gives us possible forms of co-perpetration or complicity, co-perpetration, instigation, and abetting. The concept of abetting implies the following: It implies responsibility. It implies a form of responsibility in which a person with intent abets another person in the perpetration of a crime. What was implied by abetting a person in the perpetration of a crime, rendering advice or instruction as to the manner of commission of a criminal offence, making available to the perpetrator the means for committing a criminal offence, removing obstacles to the commission of a criminal offence, and the promising before the commission of a criminal act to conceal the following: The criminal offence, the perpetrator, the means by which the crime was perpetrated, and the traces of the crime or items obtained by or through the criminal offence. Abetting entails intent. It is a deliberate act. It requires the mens rea. It requires awareness, and it requires knowledge. Abetting can take two forms. You can abet by doing or by not doing. In neither of these cases, however, for someone to be held criminally responsible, in both of these cases, rather, the perpetrator and the abettor must be mutually connected and they must be aware of each other. The perpetrator must know of the abettor and must be aware of the abettor, and vice versa, the abettor must be aware of the perpetrator. In order to establish abetting as a form of co-perpetration, it is sufficient for the abettor to know that by his actions he abets the crimes of a principal perpetrator. Finally, abetting is a deliberate action. It means intent. It entails intent. An abettor must have intent. Abetting by negligence or reckless abetting, which the law says is also an option, does not qualify as abetting in the legal sense of the word, and no person can be held criminally responsible for that. An abettor must have intent in carrying out his actions. In our jurisprudence, the jurisprudence that both my client, the accused Dragan Jokic, and I come from, intent, in the tradition of the continental law, is an action which divides into two components, direct intent and possible intent. Under the concept of direct intent, the law provides that the perpetrator should have the mens rea and that he actively wills the action to be carried out. This is the gravest form of criminal behaviour. Possibly intent, on the other hand, means that the perpetrator was in possession of the mens rea. Therefore, he was aware that by his action or as a result of his action or inaction there might result certain consequences, but he willingly agrees to the fact that these consequences may arise as a result. There is no such thing as reckless abetting. In order for someone to qualify as an abettor, he must know what the objective is, the objective of the principal perpetrator. He must have intent in abetting, this objective. Maybe this reasoning espoused by the continental legal systems is the same as the one expressed in the Brdjanin judgement, stating that in order for someone to qualify as a member of a joint criminal enterprise, there must be previous agreement or acting in concert. Your Honours, Dragan Jokic was no part to any kind of agreement. Dragan Jokic had no idea on earth what was going on in the criminal heads of a handful of people who took these monstrous decisions. Dragan Jokic's level as an officer in terms of his rank, in terms of establishment, was not high enough for someone to come up to him and tell him about these things. Dragan Jokic was not someone who was in a position to foresee the consequences that might arise from prisoners being brought to Zvornik. He does not have this evil inside his head. These consequences would never occur to any healthy and reasonable human being, namely that a large number of prisoners would be brought over, detained, and killed from the area of Srebrenica. For that reason, this Defence seeks that the Trial Chamber bring an acquittal in respect of Dragan Jokic, and that is why from the very beginning we believe that Dragan Jokic had no part in any joint criminal enterprise, that he had no mens rea to aid and abet the perpetration of these crimes. The only possible outcome would be just that, an acquittal for Dragan Jokic, to have Dragan Jokic acquitted of these charges described in the indictment. Every Defence has a bias. Please, Your Honours, allow me to take one thing at a time, paragraph by paragraph of the indictment, and to use evidence, evidence that was before you, evidence that you heard, evidence invoked by the Prosecutor to show why we seek such a sentence, a sentence of acquittal, and why that is what we believe. If we look at the substance of the indictment, paragraphs 13, 36, 46.4, 46.8, and 46.12, as well as 46.6 and 51, it follows that Dragan Jokic, as chief of engineers, directed the engineers company of the Zvornik Brigade in all the activities in which the engineers company was allegedly involved in the burials of Srebrenica's victims. The Defence has tried on a number of different occasions to draw the Trial Chamber's attention, both in writing and orally, to the problem that we encounter when we come across the term "direction." This is a term that is used throughout these cited paragraphs of the indictment. Now at the close of this trial, we again beseech you to pay attention to the fact that this is no mere semantic issue. This is an essential issue, central to Dragan Jokic's position. The concept of direction, as understood by the Prosecutor and according to the way in which it has tried to present this concept to the Trial Chamber, is explained in paragraph 46.4 of one of the amended joinder indictments where the term "direction" used in the indictment is used to charge Dragan Jokic with planning, monitoring, organising, and carrying out this broad level of responsibility attributed to the chief of engineers is not consistent with his actual powers, de facto or de jure. For that reason, we have remained adamant to have this concept clarified. This concept is used to practically usher in through the back door the possibility that Dragan Jokic exercised command in his capacity as chief of engineers. He did not have these powers, and he did not have this possibility. Finally, he was never charged with anything like that. Mr. McCloskey himself, on a number of occasions, reflected in the transcripts and during the examination of military expert Lackovic, as well as in writing in their response to a Defence 98 bis motion, asserted or confirmed that Dragan Jokic was not being charged with having issued orders or having had command responsibility as described in Article 7(3) of the Statute. I would like to say something else at this point. Yesterday, yet again, using the same arguments and invoking the testimony of members of the engineers company, my learned friend and colleague Mr. Waespi says here is evidence that Dragan Jokic did in fact issue orders. You're not charging me with having issued orders. You're not charging me with having command responsibility, yet you are trying to get this back in through the back door, in a manner of speaking. Again, we must reiterate this, Your Honours. Dragan Jokic had no power to issue orders. He could only convey orders. If you look at all this evidence, that is what you will find, that and nothing else. This is a good opportunity to repeat that direction is a function of the armed forces, providing guidance for individuals and the armed forces as a whole in carrying out certain objectives and tasks. Direction is a broader concept than command. It subsumes, among other things, command, the concept of command. Therefore, if both in the indictment and in the sentence we choose to retain that Dragan Jokic was directing, then this would seem to entail the powers of command, but he was never charged with that in the first place. According to the instruction on the work of command and staffs in paragraphs 3 and 4 of this Rule - it is a Rule that we used as both a Prosecution and Defence exhibit - these paragraphs define the concept of direction in such a way that it clearly emanates that de jure Dragan Jokic could never have directed the engineers company. Your Honours, in July 1995, the engineers company of the Zvornik Brigade had its own command structure. It had its own company commander. It had its own deputy company commander as well as platoon commanders. The system of singleness of command and subordination was undoubtedly functioning in the Zvornik Brigade at that time. Under paragraph 25 of the combat rule for companies and platoons in the engineering branch, and you have had occasion to familiarise yourselves with this rule, it was a Defence Exhibit, an engineers company can only ever be commanded by the company commander. He is in charge - and we see it clearly stated in that rule - of planning, directing, organising, and monitoring all the activities of the engineers company. This is clearly stated in the rules. And yet we are here holding the chief of engineers accountable. In terms of command, his direct superior is the brigade commander, whereas the commander of an engineers company uses his daily orders. And these daily orders are command documents to exercise sole command, I repeat, sole command and direction over the engineers company. His powers of command are not absolute. These powers must remain within the framework of the orders given by the brigade commander. In practice, it works like this: The brigade commander, having obtained the opinion of the chief of engineers, issues an order on the use of the engineers company. This order is a component part of the brigade commander's daily order. Pursuant to this order of the brigade commander and in line with the principle of the singleness of command, the commander of the engineers company uses his daily order, and, Your Honours, you have seen these Prosecution exhibits, the daily orders. So he uses his own daily order to elaborate on the order given by the command are and then proceeds to allocate specific duties to members of the engineers company or, indeed, its platoons. When speaking about these daily orders of the commander of the engineers company, and these were invoked by the Prosecutor both in their final brief and their closing argument in order to prove Dragan Jokic's responsibility, one sees that these were all signed by the company commander. Well, then, it must be clear who this document belongs to or who it was produced by. Both the Prosecutor and the Defence know full well that these daily orders were even written post facto, only after all these events. However, what we are trying to say is the following: A daily order is a document produced by the commander of the engineers company. Then it must be clear that Dragan Jokic's signature is simply nowhere to be found on those documents. What we do find is the signature of the commander of the engineers company. And the only logical conclusion that follows from that is that the document was produced by whoever signed it. It is a command document. Pursuant to the instruction on the work of commands and staffs, and pursuant to the rule on the use of the engineers branch, and these are exhibits, Your Honours, that have been used by both the Prosecutor and the Defence, Dragan Jokic as chief of engineers - I'm talking about his duties as chief of engineers - he draws up a plan of the engineers security and a map of mine explosive obstacles within the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Had these documents been found to be inaccurate or wanting, then he would be the one held responsible before this Tribunal. But he can't be held responsible for the daily orders produced by the company commander. That is not a document that was produced by him. However, these documents were not invoked during the trial simply because no such documents were produced, which clearly goes to confirm and corroborate the fact that Dragan Jokic had no part in planning this operation in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, nor was he involved in any kind of activity related to the burials of victims. This is further confirmed by the OTP's own military analyst, Mr. Butler, on page T5306 of the transcript, where he claims that he found no document that would prove that the use of the engineers branch was planned for the burials. I would like to remind you yet again, Your Honours, that there was material evidence. I refer to an attendance list for the command of the Zvornik Brigade in July 1995. This was a Prosecution Exhibit. What emanates from that exhibit is that on the 12th of July, Dragan Jokic was not in the Zvornik Brigade at all. He was elsewhere. On the 13th of July, Dragan Jokic is going about his regular duties. He's doing what God allows him to do. He prunes trees, cherry trees and apple trees in order to provide timber for the soldiers to light a fire and to keep warm. He has no idea what at that time is going on inside the heads of some people who are plotting the execution of thousands of people. Dragan Jokic could not have been further from that. On the 14th of July, with no previous planning, and we know why, Dragan Obrenovic calls him over to take over his duty. Why? Because Dragan Obrenovic, on the 13th of July, as he admits himself, knows what would be going on in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Therefore, when we speak about directing the engineers company, this whole debate merely goes to show that Dragan Jokic under no rule that exists could, de jure, have been directing the engineers company. The Prosecutor has presented no material proof. They have not produced a single witness that could confirm beyond reasonable doubt that Dragan Jokic had the powers or the authority to direct the engineers company. Any other ruling of the Court to the effect that Dragan Jokic did direct the engineers company would be contrary to these regulations that we have invoked, regulations defining his position. Moreover, it would be contrary and fly in the face of material evidence confirming that on that day, there was no doubt that the system of singleness of command and subordination did, in fact, work smoothly in the Zvornik Brigade. If I wish to remain objective, which I do, the logical question would be to ask what, then, was Dragan Jokic doing in his capacity as chief of engineers? The Defence does not challenge the fact that he was a staff officer, that he was chief of engineers, or that he was directly subordinated to the chief of the Zvornik Brigade, Dragan Obrenovic. The de jure definition of his position and duties is enshrined, first of all, by paragraph 120 of the rule on brigades, which is Prosecution Exhibit P83, stating that the branch organ in the brigade is a technical organ advising on the most effective use of units belonging to the different branches, so that the brigade as a whole could complete its task in the best possible way. The chief of engineers is the one who advises the commander and makes proposals on the use of the engineers units, but he does not direct the engineers unit. The next set of regulations defining the position of Dragan Jokic as chief of engineers is the rule on the use of engineers, which is Defence Exhibit D23, which we refer to as the lex specialis in relation to the chief of engineers. Paragraph 40 contains a detailed index of the duties and powers of the chief of engineers. This is no need for us to quote this rule again because the rule is available to the Honourable Trial Chamber. However, the rule spells out in no uncertain terms that the chief of engineers cannot direct the engineers company, particularly if an organised command structure is in fact in place within the engineers company. The third document defining the position of the chief of engineers is the rules governing the competences of commanders from brigade to regiment level. This is a Defence Exhibit, D72/3. In paragraph 69, it states that branch organs enjoy all the rights of a superior officer in relation to units belonging to their branch. And now I must emphasise. It goes on to state "except the right to use them." They have no right to actually use the unit. Is there anything more direct that we can say? All these exhibits clearly describe the position of Dragan Jokic as chief of engineers. They indicate clearly that de jure, and later on we will go on to discuss de facto, but de jure he could absolutely not direct the engineers. Had Dragan Jokic taken on greater authority than provided for in the rules, he would either have been acting as a renegade commander violating the rules of singleness of command and subordination, and I assure you that he could never have done this or would never have dared to do this in the presence of Pandurevic, Obrenovic, and the others, or this would have been behaviour for which Dragan Jokic would have had to have special authorisation from the brigade commander, and this would have had to be in writing. We are now coming to the evidence adduced by the Prosecution. They say yes, that is how it is de jure, but it's not like that de facto. De facto he was able to direct the troops. And they refer to a segment of the Dragan Obrenovic's testimony when he said that Vinko Pandurevic, as brigade commander, orally told Dragan Jokic that he could take on certain competences in commanding the engineers company because the commander of the engineering company, Dragan Jevtic, had no military training. This argument -- or, rather, this thesis of Dragan Obrenovic's is not corroborated by single shred of evidence produced by the Prosecution. All we have is Obrenovic's statement. Moreover, the military expert of the Prosecution, Mr. Butler, on the record of the 24th of November, I remember it was in the afternoon in Courtroom II, on page 5239 confirmed this and said there was no written order in existence on the transfer of authority from the commander of the engineers company to the chief of engineers. This same military expert says that such a transfer of authority, in his view, would have had to be in writing, because it takes away the prerogatives of command from the commander of the engineering company. It is contrary to the rules, and for this reason the commander of the engineers company would have had to have been informed of it. Your Honours, we have had occasion to hear the testimony of Witness Minja Radovic. He was the commander of the engineers company from 1992 to early June 1995. As commander of the engineers company, he said, "No one ever took away from me, as a commander, my authority to command. Dragan Jokic could not have issued orders to me. He could only have conveyed orders." He said, "In the engineers company I had greater authority than Dragan Jokic did." Where is the evidence to corroborate Obrenovic's statement? Perhaps now is the time, Your Honours, to remind you that we heard testimony corroborating that Dragan Jevtic who was then commander of the engineers company and with whom I mention with respect, was not a common private in the JNA. He was a company leader. In his civilian life, he was a civil engineer. He had a university degree, and he was better equipped than Dragan Jokic to know how, in what way to use building construction machinery. His deputy, Slavko Bogicevic, was a mechanical engineer in his civilian life, which means that he was also fully trained and equipped to supervise the operation of building construction machines. Therefore, there is not a shred of corroborating evidence to support Obrenovic's statement. Secondly -- the second point I wish to make to show that what Obrenovic said was not true is the following: If the brigade commander transferred command authority over the engineers company to Dragan Jokic, had he done this, the daily orders of the engineers company commander would have been signed by the chief of engineers, because he would also have been the commander of the engineers company. But they were not signed by him, Your Honours. You have them before you. They were signed by the commander of the engineers company. Why? Because he was the one commanding the engineers company. Even when he came back from the front line, he signed these orders retroactively. Dragan Jokic did not sign any of them. There is no evidence that this authority was ever transferred to Dragan Jokic. There is not a single argument to support Dragan Obrenovic's thesis. As for the quality and truthfulness of the Dragan Obrenovic's testimony, we will return to this in this closing statement. This Defence considers that such testimony and such a witness is not something on which one can found any decision or any judgement which aspires to establish the truth about the events in Srebrenica. If all this is confirmed by Mr. Butler, who I assure you is not kindly deposed towards the Defence, and if he says there is no evidence to prove this, there is no written order on the transfer of authority. If the commander of the engineers company also says this, then the matter is quite clear. Dragan Jokic never took on the authority of commanding the engineers company. Your Honours, look at the situation the Defence finds itself in again. I am constantly bearing in mind your instruction as to the relevance of command authority and who was in command, but I have to defend my client from charges that have to do with command. I am again having to defend Jokic from Article 7(3) of the Statute. This was set out the day before yesterday in the closing argument, although I know that Jokic is not charged with command responsibility. But the final argument of the Prosecutor contains arguments purporting to aggravate the sentence of Dragan Jokic, and this I find very painful. Your Honours, I wish to go on and say that the competencies of the chief of engineers indicate clearly that Dragan Jokic, in view of his character, in view of his personality structure, was not a person who could issue commands. He was an officer of a different type. He gave a personal example. He preferred to carry out the orders of the brigade commander himself rather than convey them to the engineers company. You will remember a testimony here which was very convincing. Witness Branko Mihic said that he was embarrassed to see Vinko Pandurevic, the brigade commander, issuing an order to Dragan Jokic, his staff officer, telling him to dig a trench. And he did so without any objection. This is not an officer with authority to issue orders. Dragan Jokic's duty was to advise the commander or the Chief of Staff on the most effective use of the engineers company, and I cannot deny, and because I wish the truth to be established, I have to say that yes, it was his duty to convey orders, when the commander required him to, to the engineers company. He was duty-bound to take care of the training and equipment of the engineers company. It was the brigade commander, Your Honours, who could either take his advice on the use of the engineers or not. I will remind you of the testimonies of Witness (redacted), the military expert Lackovic, and Butler, who all said that according to paragraph 114 of the guidelines on the works -- on the work of commands and staffs, when there was surprise activities by the enemy during combat or sudden changes in the situation and in other circumstances when there is no time to consult the command organs, the commander can, without any consultation with the chief of engineers, issue an order on the use of the engineers company. Bearing in mind the position of Dragan Jokic, the authority he had with Vinko Pandurevic and his very poor relations with his direct superior, Dragan Obrenovic, situations in which the commander accepted Dragan Jokic's suggestions or advice were rare. Therefore, in the view of this Defence, Dragan Jokic cannot be found guilty of activities entailing the authority to direct the engineers company because he simply did not have the authority to do this. This is the legal framework, Your Honours, regulating the issue of whether the chief of engineers can direct the engineers company. However, we have had quite a lot of evidence here as to the de facto role of Dragan Jokic, and this has been invoked by the Prosecution in their closing argument. I will attempt very briefly, paragraph by paragraph, wherever direction of the engineers is mentioned and Dragan Jokic, to go through this and carry out a synthesis of the evidence invoked by the Prosecution in order to show that Dragan Jokic did not exercise authority to direct the engineers company de facto. Your Honours, this might be a good point to take a break, because I will now move on to talk about the de facto authority and actions of Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, we are in your hands concerning the breaks. If you believe that it is now convenient to break now, we will take 30 minutes break, and we will resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Let me remind you that we left off just as I was about to speak about particular paragraphs in the indictment. In paragraph 46.4 of the amended joinder indictment, Dragan Jokic is charged by the Prosecutor with directing the troops, the troops, let me reiterate, of the Zvornik Brigade who participated in the operation of removing and burying the bodies of Srebrenica Muslims in the Kravica warehouse. In support of this claim, the Prosecution produces the statement of Witness P178, who at the time was a member of the engineers company. During his testimony on the 4th and 5th of December, 2003, this witness confirmed that driving a truck, he took part in the transportation of the corpses of Srebrenica Muslims from the Kravica warehouse to the mass grave in Glogova, and that on the 15th of July, in the afternoon, he carried out this task. Well, now, let's try to analyse this piece of evidence which is the only piece of evidence the Prosecution has on the participation of this unit of the Zvornik Brigade. This Prosecution witness says that he was the only one from the Zvornik Brigade who was there working on the transportation of bodies from Kravica to Glogova. So we cannot speak of troops. There is only a private. However, troops are mentioned in the indictment. My second point is: Was Dragan Jokic directing this private of the Zvornik company? I have already said that de jure he neither could have done this nor did he do it. Did he do it de facto? In the view is of the Defence, he did not. This is the only conclusion that can be drawn from this evidence. Why do I say this? It was precisely this witness, Prosecution Witness P178 who said, "On the 14th of July, 1995, Dragan Jokic instructed me to report to the civilian protection in Zvornik where I would take the truck because it was necessary for me to spend several days on the ground cleaning up the town of Srebrenica." This witness confirms that knowing Dragan Jokic well and being familiar with his position in the brigade, it was quite clear to him that this decision on him being sent and put at the disposal of the Zvornik civilian protection - I'm referring to the witness and the truck - that this decision could not have been made by Dragan Jokic. I quote the witness. He said, "I and the truck were put at the disposal of the civilian protection, and this had to be done through the brigade. It had to go through the superior officers of the brigade." This is transcript page T5693, Your Honours. After this witness reported to the civilian protection in Zvornik, and after having spent some time in front of the municipal building in Zvornik together with Arsen Krunic, Dragan Mirkovic, and Rajko Djokic, who were members of the Zvornik civilian protection or the republican civilian protection staff of Republika Srpska, he went to Bratunac where the three of them spent the entire afternoon. And then Rajko Djokic told him he could not go to Srebrenica because it would not be safe for them to clean the streets of the town until the remaining mines were removed. He spent the night in a hotel, and on the afternoon of the 15th, a day and a half after having spoken to Jokic, after the meeting of the civilian protection in Bratunac had ended, a member of the civilian protection took him to the village of Kravica without telling him what he was to do there. On his arrival in Kravica, he was told that he had to transport these corpses. He did this, and there were other members of the Bratunac civilian protection working on the same assignment. And in the evening, he conveyed to Rajko Djokic, who on the previous day had told him that it was not possible to enter Srebrenica, he told him that he did not wish to participate in this job. Rajko Djokic, whom you were able to hear testifying here, corroborated this and said, "We didn't come there to do this kind of job. We're abandoning this job." And on the 16th of July, 1995, in the morning, they left Bratunac. Witness P178, as mentioned by the Prosecution in their closing argument, said that on the 17th of July he spoke to Dragan Jokic and told him what he had been doing. What did Jokic reply? I repeat this. He told him that he had conveyed to him the order - and this is what we are not challenging - to go and carry out a completely different task, not the task that he was assigned by the civilian protection in Bratunac. This witness directly states that Dragan Jokic could not assign any member of the engineers company without the knowledge and approval of the brigade commander or of the engineers company commander. He could not give him any assignment or give him leave. He could only convey an order. And this follows clearly from the testimony of this witness who confirms this on page T5693. Your Honours, where in all this is Dragan Jokic? Where do we see him directing Witness P178 to do the work in Kravica? The answer is clear. Dragan Jokic is not present in this activity. He only conveyed the order that the witness should go to the Zvornik civilian protection and report together with the vehicle he was driving. From there, others sent him to Bratunac. The day after that, it was a third set of people who directed him to go to Kravica. This witness says, when questioned by the Prosecutor, "I did not contact Dragan Jokic. It was not possible for me to contact him in those few days. My first meeting with Jokic after this was on the 17th." He said, "I was sent to clean up Srebrenica, not to transport corpses. I do not wish to be an undertaker." And he left that assignment on the following morning. He abandoned it. Let's look at the remaining -- at the other evidence. After your 98 bis decision, Witness Rajko Djokic was examined. You will remember him. He was an elderly man, a teacher, and everything that Witness P178 said, he corroborated. Moreover, this witness confirmed that he was superior to P178, not Dragan Jokic. You can see this on pages 11898 and 11899 from his examination. He was the one who said he was in charge. He was the one who was superior to Witness P178. Do we have any other evidence about this? Yes. Defence witness for Mr. Blagojevic, P501, who was chief of the civilian protection --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology, D101.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D101 also speaks about these sanitisation activities, and he says that it was the civilian protection of Bratunac that was in charge of this task. Finally, bearing in mind the rules regulating resubordination, then it is clear that Dragan Jokic cannot direct the activities of soldier P178 at the Kravica warehouse. Both military experts, that is to say both Mr. Butler as a Prosecution expert, and Mr. Lackovic as a Defence expert, confirm that a soldier who is resubordinated to another unit or another military or civilian structure, from the point of view of discipline - discipline is the word that Mr. Butler used - he reports to the officer that he had been resubordinated to, or, rather, the unit that he works for at that point in time and not to the officer of the -- the commanding officer of the unit that he came from. Your Honours, you can read that on page 5225 of the transcript of Mr. Butler's evidence, and from Mr. Lackovic on page 12133 and 12134. To put it in very simple terms, if as a commanding officer officer, I send a soldier to another unit to carry out a particular assignment and then in the other unit he gets a new assignment which is indeed a war crime, I am not the one who is held responsible. The person who gave him that task is held responsible from the point of view of discipline. That is proof and evidence as far as paragraph 46.4 is concerned. There is no other evidence. Attempts had been made here through travel forms, travel authorisation forms, et cetera, to say that this witness was in Orahovac at that time. That, quite simply, is not true. On the -- that this witness was in Orahovac on the 14th. No. They say this witness was in Kravica. And what the travel form said was only for the sake of fuel. So I don't want to make the establishment of the truth any more difficult than it is, because the situation is clear cut. Also, Your Honours, Witness 178, Witness P101, Witness Rajko Djokic, the experts, Mr. Butler, that is, and Mr. Lackovic, and the regulations I referred to earlier on confirm that Dragan Jokic, from the point of view of paragraph 46.4 of the indictment, is not involved in directing either soldiers -- or, rather, troops, as the indictment says, or a soldier from the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade in the transport of the corporations from Kravica to the mass grave in Glogova. Therefore, I ask you, Your Honours, precisely for those reasons, because I don't know of any others, reject the factual basis of 46.4 -- paragraph 46.4 of the amended rejoinder indictment of Dragan Jokic. Let us move further on. Paragraph 46.6 of the indictment says that Dragan Jokic directed the members of the engineering company when, on the 14th and 15th of July, 1995, they used heavy equipment to bury the victims of mass executions in mass graves at execution sites themselves. What is it that the Prosecution put before the Trial Chamber in order to corroborate this? The statement of Cvijetin Ristanovic, a member of the engineering company. And as for material evidence, travel forms and also the daily orders of the engineering company. Let us analyse this evidence. We continue to assert de jure, according to regulations, Dragan Jokic does not direct the engineers. Does he direct Cvijetin Ristanovic at that point in time? This Defence says, and we will dwell on the subject more later on as well, Dragan Jokic, in the afternoon of the 14th of July, is not aware that the prisoners in Orahovac will be executed, and in that sense, he could not have participated in this crime. As for whether he had knowledge, we shall speak about that further on. Now we're just saying that he was not engaged in direction. Witness Cvijetin Ristanovic, in his testimony on page 5406 and 5407, says that at one point in time on the 14th of July, Dragan Jokic came to the engineering and told him to go to the school in Orahovac and to take on the platform trailer the excavator 07 and to take it to the school in Orahovac. This witness says that on that occasion, "Dragan Jokic did not tell me what I was supposed to do there." Further on, he says that he did come to the school in Orahovac, that that is where he found some trucks that were turning around. Also, there were soldiers in camouflage uniforms and military police, that he did not know which unit they belonged to. At one point in time, he was told to go on to the fountain which was about one kilometre away from the school. Your Honours, you were on site yourselves, and you saw where the school is and where the fountain is. That fits into what the witness has been saying. This witness says, to the best of his recollection, that that is where the deputy commander of the engineers company was, and that he issued him an order to go underneath the flyover. You remember the flyover, don't you? And he indicated to him the spot where the pit was supposed to be dug. That is what he did. At one point in time while the pit was being dug, unknown soldiers and officers told him to stop doing that and to go away for a while. Precisely it is at that moment that the execution of the Srebrenica victims started. This witness says further on, the following day, the 15th, in the morning, he received an order again from his platoon commander - note that, his platoon commander - to go to Orahovac and to continue digging the pit. This platoon commander went with him to Orahovac, and that is where he came across several people from the civilian protection and from the Zvornik public utility company, and they were burying the bodies in the graves that they had dug. This witness confirms that not a -- not at a single point in time did he see Dragan Jokic in Orahovac. Also, he was adamant in his claim that Dragan Jokic had not said anything to him on the 14th of July in terms of what he was supposed to do in Orahovac. That is the testimony of that witness. The daily orders book that we already referred to of the commander of the engineering company refers to that and confirms what this witness said, that the excavator, and now for the transcript BGH700, on that day, the 14th of July, 1995, was working in Orahovac. Also, the vehicle records or log sheets that the Prosecution uses also confirm this fact. The Defence is not denying that either. It is correct that on that day, this machine, regardless of whether it was called BGH700 or RD700, that is of lesser importance, but this machine was in Orahovac, and it was working on the big -- on the digging of these pits or graves. But where is there evidence of Dragan Jokic directing of the -- directing the members of the engineers company in Orahovac? The answer is that Dragan Jokic is not there and that there is no evidence to that effect. Dragan Jokic could only convey, as duty operations officer, convey, yet again, convey only the order of the Chief of Staff, Dragan Obrenovic, that this engineering machine be sent to Orahovac. Dragan Obrenovic himself admit that precisely on that day, the 14th of July, he let two machinists go from the positions on Snagovo, on that day. You have that in his plea agreement, Your Honours. Because he knew that they were supposed to go to Orahovac to dig and to bury the killed persons. He admits that. Obrenovic also admits that already on the 13th of July, in the evening hours, he had received information that a large number of prisoners of war would be brought to the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade and that they would be killed. He admits that he accepted and supported that activity and that he made the resources of the Zvornik Brigade available for this operation. Where is Dragan Jokic there? As the witness says, he conveyed the order to Witness Cvijetin Ristanovic to take the BGH to the school in Orahovac. Does Dragan Jokic know what is supposed to happen in Orahovac at that point in time? There is already historical information that the executions started in the afternoon. The Prosecution did not proffer such evidence, and we are going to refer to that later on, to a particular statement related to this matter. This same Prosecution witness confirms that the order, in terms of what he was supposed to do in Orahovac, he received from the deputy commander of the engineering company on the 14th of July, and what he was supposed to do on the 15th of July was what he heard through orders from his platoon commander. This is direct evidence that the system of command and control in the engineering company of the Zvornik Brigade was fully operational on the basis of the principle of subordination at that. Obrenovic, the deputy commander of the engineering company, the platoon commander, and then ultimately the soldier who carries this out. It is as clear-cut as can be. Nobody is denying that. By the way, Cvijetin Ristanovic is not the operator of that excavator, and he is not the machinist for BGH700. It was Milovan Miladinovic who was in charge of this machine. So he is the only one who could have received orders to operate the machine, which is indeed what happened on the afternoon of the 14th. Cvijetin Ristanovic does testify about that. That is precisely the reason why Dragan Obrenovic let this operator, this machinist, go for Snagovo to Orahovac. Obrenovic knows who is in charge of that machine, and that is Miladinovic. The daily order of the engineering company to send the excavator to Orahovac was signed by the commander of the engineering company, not Dragan Jokic. This confirms yet again that Dragan Jokic cannot de facto direct the engineering company or issue any orders to that effect. If I'm guilty because I conveyed an order which does constitute a crime, if the crime is digging pits for persons to be buried in, then I have to have knowledge of that. I have to have mens rea to the effect that I am conveying an evil order. We are going to deal with this later on as well, Your Honours. I have not omitted that. When the Prosecution says in paragraph 46 of the indictment members of the engineering company buried the victims of the mass executions, that is quite pretentious. It says in paragraph 46 that it was members who -- of the engineering company who buried them. But that's not what the engineering company did. That is what witnesses have attested to as well. This is something that many persons took part in. This same Prosecution witness says that burials were carried out by the members of the civilian protection of Zvornik and the public utilities company of Zvornik, and that it is true that he participated in the burial operation, too, by operating the machine that was actually digging the hole itself. Why am I saying this? This is a very hard story. I simply would like you to realise that the operation of burial was not only under the engineers company. The public utilities company took part in it, the civilian protection, the logistics people of the Zvornik Brigade, and the engineers. Can Dragan Jokic direct all these structures, all these participants? He cannot. That's what Mr. Butler says too. That is what Mr. Lackovic says. Only a person with far greater authority can direct so many different participants. It is only the commander of the brigade or the Chief of Staff or perhaps the assistant commander for logistics, as Mr. Butler says. Only they could do that. However, wherever the machine appeared in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade, there is invariably reference to Dragan Jokic. That is the way the indictment against Dragan Jokic was conceived. On the basis of all the above, if we try to make a synthesis of all this evidence, if we look at all these pieces of evidence individually or accumulatively, we cannot come to a different conclusion but one, and that is that Dragan Jokic did not direct the engineering company in the operation of the burial of the victims in Orahovac. Hence, this factual allegation from the allegation, in our modest opinion, should be rejected. As far as paragraph 46.8 of the indictment is concerned, Your Honours, what we believe is spelled out in even more radical terms. It says that he directed the engineers company and that he, together with other individuals, used an excavator and other heavy machinery to bury, on the morning of the 15th, the victims of the mass execution near the Petkovci dam in the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. You had the opportunity of seeing the actual site. It looks quite horrifying until the present day. We also had the opportunity of hearing the testimony of a survivor of that execution here, and this was very hurtful testimony. It was very hard. It is very hard on all of us who are engaged in this job of the Defence, that we should not act in haste, that we should not overstep in any way. The witness says yes, the construction machine which was there, and the Prosecution uses that. Is there more evidence about that? The Prosecution says yes, there is material evidence. The daily orders of the commander of the engineers company, that two machines, the ULT220 and the excavator, on that day, the 15th of July, operated in Petkovci. This Defence wishes to analyse this once again, Your Honours. I cannot deny the fact that certain construction machinery was there at the time. That would be senseless. But I can challenge that these machines belong to the engineering company, and that is what I wish to say here. First of all, in this daily order there is reference to the ULT220 construction machine. Again, the daily order was signed by Dragan Jokic. The daily order was signed by the commander of the engineering company. That is his order. Just for the transcript, let me repeat: The daily order was not signed by Dragan Jokic. It was signed by the commander of the engineering company. Who operated these machines? Were they members of the engineers company? The Prosecution did not adduce any evidence to that effect. Can the machines operate on their own? They cannot. Who is operating these machines? This Defence says, although the burden of proof lies with the Prosecution, that these machines were operated by persons who were civilians. These were machines that were mobilised from civilian life, Your Honours. As these machines were mobilised, Dragan Jokic had nothing to do with that whatsoever. You heard the testimony of military experts here, that is to say Mr. Butler and Mr. Lackovic. They confirm that the mobilisation of machines is carried out by the department of the Ministry of Defence of the municipality of Zvornik at the proposal of and at the request of the commander or Chief of Staff of the Zvornik Brigade. This is also confirmed by witnesses, Minja Radovic, who was commander of the engineers company of the Zvornik Brigade, and Witness Tesic Aleksandar, the witness of the Defence who was head of defence in Bratunac. So we do not have any evidence before this Honourable Trial Chamber about who operated these machines. We have other evidence, a summary of the engineers' activities, the Defence Exhibit 12/3, where we find all the machines and all the equipment available to the engineers company described in detail. It clearly shows that there is no such machine available as a ULT220. So where did it come from, and how could Jokic possibly have been in charge of this particular piece of machinery? There is no answer to that. It's sufficient to have a theory that Jokic was directing the engineers, that this was a machine which belonged to the engineers company, that it was in a daily order of the engineers company, and this should be quite sufficient to conclude that Jokic is guilty. Your Honours, the Defence believes that this is not possible. No one ever saw Jokic anywhere near that place. There was another piece of machinery in the daily order, an excavator. Your Honours, according to the same summary, an overview that was provided to us by the OTP, the engineers company only had one excavator, the BG700. On the 15th of July, this excavator was in Orahovac, which was confirmed by Cvijetin Ristanovic who was actually operating this piece of machinery. How then could this piece of machinery be in Petkovci at the same time? Well, it wasn't. There was a different machine that was there that had been mobilised from a civilian structure who had mobilised those machines and who had sent them to Petkovci. A person knew what was going on in Petkovci and who was aware of the crimes. And I'm telling you it is P130, Witness P130. Only time will show how exactly this unfolded. But, Your Honours, one thing is for sure, Dragan Jokic is nowhere to be found. Therefore, the Prosecutor has provided no evidence beyond reasonable doubt that the machines belonging to the engineers company or its members were indeed involved in the burials at Petkovci. What's more, they could certainly not offer any evidence that Dragan Jokic, in his capacity as chief of engineers, during the night between the 14th and 15th of July and on the morning of the 15th, while he was on duty as the operations duty officer back at the brigade, that he was indeed in charge of that engineering operation. Too many things being said about Dragan Jokic. Perhaps this is a good opportunity, Your Honour, following this analysis of Dragan Jokic's de facto role in the events at Orahovac and Petkovci, to reiterate a position of the Defence, a position that we have presented a number of times throughout the trial. While an officer is on duty as an operations duty officer, all his other functional duties cease to apply, the duties that he had abandoned once he took over his duty as the operations duty officer. Two days ago in their closing argument, the Prosecution rejected this theory, and they also rejected this theory in their final brief. What do they state in support of their own position? They cite parts of certain daily orders and the testimony of Witness Cvijetin Ristanovic and Witness P178 as well as the intercept dated 2110 hours, the 14th of July, 1995. However, we are adamant that none of these allegations made by the Prosecutor are in any way sufficient to deny the simple fact that in compliance with the regulations and according to what the actual state of affairs was, it was impossible for Dragan Jokic to discharge both duties. What do the regulations tell us about this? Paragraph 202 of the rules on service in the armed forces. This is Defence Exhibit D71/3 state as follows: I will quote this because it is a single sentence: "The organs of internal service, and this is also applies to the duty operations officer cannot, cannot while on duty discharge other activities that are not related to their duty." This is as clear as possible by way of an answer. The rule is crystal clear. I am the duty operations officer. Therefore, I cannot discharge any other functional duties. The military expert, Dragoslav Lackovic, in his written report states that Dragan Jokic's takeover of duty as duty operations officer on the 14th of July, 1995 virtually meant that he was receiving a short-term transfer to a different duty, and he could not at the same time act as chief of engineers. Accordingly, the Prosecutor must decide what they're charging Dragan Jokic with on the 14th and 15th of July. Are they charging him in his capacity as duty operations officer or in his capacity as chief of engineers? That is as long as we wish to abide by the rules. Once we choose not it abide by the rules, we can go on to deal with the de facto situation. What follows from this theory of the Prosecution is that their selection of charges was rather poor. "We'll charge wherever we think we can." It is up to the Chamber to pick the charges that are eventually proved beyond reasonable doubt. Based on all the evidence that we have produced, this Defence still believes, and there haven't been so many different sets of evidence because virtually both the Prosecutor and the Defence are speaking about the same things, based on all of that, there is not sufficient evidence to prove beyond reasonable discount that the engineers company or the members of the engineers company were involved in the burials alongside with other individuals and other units at the Petkovci dam. In particular, there is no proof that Dragan Jokic was directing this operation. This allegation from paragraph 46.8 of the amended joinder indictment must, therefore, also be rejected. As for paragraphs 46.9, 46.10, and 46.11, they refer to the burials of victims near the Kula school, the cultural centre at Pilica, and the military farm at Branjevo. We have visited all these places, and yet in all three of these paragraphs in the indictment it is stated that the engineers company, alongside with other individuals and units, took part in the burials by digging the graves, and it is stated that Dragan Jokic was directing their work. What is the OTP's evidence to prove that Dragan Jokic did de facto direct this operation? Again we have Cvijetin Ristanovic's testimony. We have Drazen Erdemovic's testimony. We have the testimony of Witness P130. We have material evidence. We have vehicle records and log sheets, and again a daily order from the commander of the engineers company. Finally, we have the logbook containing the entries made by the duty operations officer, Prosecution Exhibit P133 in relation to the 16th. Your Honours, let us try to sum this up and analyse it as briefly as possible. We shall not address all the details, all the allegations and all the statements of these witnesses which we have already commented on in our final brief, but we do wish to point out a number of essential facts. On the 16th of July, 1995, when the burial of victims at the Branjevo Military Farm took place, no one saw Dragan Jokic there. No one ever said they did. None of the members of the engineers company, and we do know that Cvijetin Ristanovic was there, because that's what he testified, none of them have actually confirmed that Dragan Jokic was the one who sent them to Branjevo. Quite the contrary. We have a Prosecution witness, Cvijetin Ristanovic, who clearly says that he had received the order to go to Branjevo from his own platoon commander of the engineering -- of the engineers company, and that this platoon commander was, in fact, present when the mass grave was being dug. That is what the witness stated. You can read that on pages T5389 and again on pages T5418 and T5419. He did not see Dragan Jokic, nor did Dragan Jokic issue any orders to him or indeed convey to him an order that he should go to Branjevo. This fact is confirmed by the OTP's military expert, Mr. Butler, who says that during years of work in this case, he never found any evidence showing that Dragan Jokic was present at these places where the burials took place between the 14th and the 18th of July, 1995. He claims to have found no evidence whatsoever to that effect. This is on page T5212 of the transcript, Your Honours. Prosecution witnesses that were heard confirmed that Dragan Jokic was not in any way involved with the engineering machines at Branjevo. So where was Dragan Jokic, Your Honours? On that day, the 17th of July, 1995, he was at the other end of the zone of defence of the Zvornik defence. He was linking up the lines and controlling the minefield in an area called Gresnik. This may be a symbolical thing. Gresnik in B/C/S means sinner. Again, we see Dragan Jokic going there to do the work of an ordinary soldier, controlling the minefield, and he was not alone with this. Also involved were the members of the pioneers platoon of the engineers company, and we heard Brano Djuric's testimony to that effect. As a foot soldier, he's there with the members of the engineers company involved in this kind of work. At the same time there is someone else who is coordinating, who is issuing orders, and who is digging the pits at Branjevo. And then we have the indictment that tells us everything was done under the direction of Dragan Jokic. No, it wasn't. There is no other possible answer. The daily order of the commander of the engineers company, I must come back to this because the Prosecutor seems to be constantly referring to it. This daily order tells that the excavator went to Branjevo. We are not disputing that. The excavator was there operated by Cvijetin Ristanovic, and pursuant to the same order, his commander was there too. Again, who signed this daily order? The company commander did, not Dragan Jokic. How, then, could Dragan Jokic possibly have been in charge or directing that? And there is no answer. And the OTP provides no answer. If I may draw your attention to another bit of evidence referred to by Mr. Waespi, the testimony of Witness P130 and his alleged entry in the duty operations officer's logbook in relation to the 16th of July, 1995, where he states that there have been requests from the 1st Infantry Battalion to have a truck and an excavator secured for the next day. What happens then? P130 makes a note to the effect that Dragan Jokic should be, in the future tense, informed and Sreten Jokic [as interpreted] about this request. Even if this was the case, what did that mean? Did he eventually inform them about that or not? Did Dragan Jokic do anything about that? You have a witness who very clearly states who was the one who sent him to Branjevo. It's an OTP witness. This is where we should come back to the testimony of Witness P130, and we will keep come back to it in our closing arguments. As for his testimony, as for the authenticity of his statement, as for the fact that he, Your Honours, lied to you under oath during his testimony on the 26th, 27th, and 28th of January, the Defence has spoken sufficiently about this in our final brief. We would not like to go back to that now. We continue to submit that no ruling can be based on the testimony of this witness, Witness P130. This witness himself admits that he did not tell the truth before this Honourable Trial Chamber, although he was aware of his duty to do so. We will come back to this witness in relation to a key issue, namely was Dragan Jokic aware of the objective of the joint criminal enterprise as something that could be foreseen and that he, in fact, aided and abetted that operation. But here I'm referring to specific paragraphs the indictment. It is clear that Dragan Jokic was not directing the engineers company in the burials of victims at the Branjevo Military Farm. In that light, according to this Defence's humble opinion, the Trial Chamber should reject all factual allegations contained in paragraphs 46.9, 46.10, and 46.11 of the indictment. Finally, Your Honours, we have paragraph 46.12 to deal with. Again, by rote we see that the engineers company, under the direction of Dragan Jokic, alongside with other individuals and units, buried the victims of executions on the 16th of July. Buried. That is actually what it says. And that burial took place at Kozluk. What is the evidence that the OTP have proffered in relation to Dragan Jokic's de facto responsibility? We have referred already several times to the daily order of the commander of the engineers company and the testimony of OTP witness Milos Mitrovic, who was a member of the engineers company. Let us now analyse specifically what this witness claims. He confirms that on the 16th of July, 1995, Dragan Jokic conveyed to him the order that he was to take the skip torpedo machine and go to Kozluk. Again, he conveyed to him the order. This witness did not know why his presence was required in Kozluk. The same witness goes on to say that Dragan Jokic never told him what he was to do in Kozluk. Therefore, he could not confirm that Dragan Jokic in any way knew what he would be expected to do in Kozluk. What's more, this witness confirms that Dragan Jokic did not have the power to issue orders to the members of the engineers company. He merely conveyed to them the orders that had been issued by the command of the engineers company. This clearly transpires from the transcript of his testimony on pages T5618 and T5619. Further, this witness claims that upon his arrival in Kozluk, he was met by the commander of the transport platoon of the engineers company and that he issued him a specific order. Mind you, the system is functioning smoothly all the time. And the order was to take the unsealed road to the Drina riverbed as far as a pit that had been earlier been dug for gravel reclamation and to bury the victims' bodies there, the bodies of the victims that had been killed earlier on. The witness says, "As I was unable to carry out this task because the machine I had was small, it had a very small bucket. An hour -- an hour later there was another machine that came along mobilised from a civilian -- civilian structure, and it was a ULT220," the same system applies. And the witness says that this is a machine that came from the stone quarry at Josanica, and that this machine eventually buried the victims. This witness confirms that neither the machine nor the operator belonged to the engineers company. Therefore, the testimony of this witness also confirms that Dragan Jokic could not have been directing the engineers company and that he issued no orders to that effect. If we accept the testimony of Milos Mitrovic, Your Honours, then it is perfectly clear that Dragan Jokic did not know why this machine had been sent to Kozluk, because if he had known anything like that, he would have told Milos Mitrovic. With the arrival of the construction machine from a civilian source, this is something that Dragan Jokic had nothing to do with. It was stated quite clearly that Dragan Jokic did not have the power to commandeer that machine, nor did he participate in the process of mobilising it. Let me remind you again the daily order of the commander of the engineers company was signed by the commander of the engineers company, not by Dragan Jokic. Let me remind you again that Dragan Jokic is nowhere to be found in all this according to Mr. Butler. How then was he directing the skip and Milos Mitrovic? Direction includes planning, organising, commanding, and supervising or monitoring. None of this is to be found in the actions of Dragan Jokic. Therefore, this factual allegation from paragraph 46.12 should be rejected. And to conclude this topic with paragraph 51 of the indictment, it again states that the engineering company acted under the direction of Dragan Jokic in the operation of reburial from October to November 1995. What is the evidence adduced by the Prosecution? You heard in Mr. Waespi's closing argument that there is circumstantial evidence and direct evidence. The circumstantial evidence is that if you know that the engineers dug the pits, they were the ones who knew where they were, so it would have been natural for them to dig them up again. That was the deduction. That was their hypothesis. This is not evidence, not at least evidence that a reasonable trier of fact could use to establish guilt. They cannot establish the involvement of the company let alone that Dragan Jokic was in charge of the operation. Yesterday there was mention of the quality of the circumstantial evidence, so there is not need to reiterate this point. But, Your Honours, I wish to remind you that both in the trial judgement and the appeal judgement in the Krstic case, if I remember correctly, I think it's in paragraph 241 or 261 of the Krstic judgement, it was stated that the Trial Chamber had not proved beyond reasonable doubt that members and units of the Drina Corps to which the Zvornik Brigade belongs participated in this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to any discussion on the factual findings of the Krstic Trial Chamber or the Appellate Chamber. Legal findings I have no problem with, but as you know there have been many factual findings, and I don't think we want to open that door for the Prosecution to go through nor the Defence because it is a very large door and there are many facts. We have been through the process of motions for adjudicated facts and that process has ended, but to open up the actual factual findings of the Krstic judgement I think -- I would object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic. I believe that you said, if I remember it correctly, we'll check with this part, that we should touch as less as possible about the facts findings in other judgements. And at the same time, please believe us that we will arrive at our conclusion concerning with certain facts based on the evidence we received from this trial. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do not wish to say that this Trial Chamber should rely on the facts established there. I just wish to point out that that's what happened, but I think that this was not challenged. However, let us go back to the other piece of evidence that the Prosecution feels is relevant to prove that Dragan Jokic directed the reburial operation. This is the testimony of Witness P130, Your Honours. This witness spoke at length and extensively. He gave the Defence a lot of trouble, and we have discussed him at length in our closing brief. Therefore, I will now refer to him only briefly and to his testimony, but allow me to do so after the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It is time for the break. We are adjourned until 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. If you will allow me, I have been told that we have some minor corrections to make in the transcript, so I wish to do so on the record now. In line 40.1, instead of Exhibit T70/3, it should say D71/3. In the transcript, in line 44.3, instead of the words Sreten Jokic, it should say Sreten Milosevic. In line 44.13, it says in the transcript Milos Mitrovic, commander, and then there is a gap. Milos Mitrovic was a member of the engineers company, the road platoon. And in line 47.11, it says from October to November 1995. It should say from August to November 1995. And in the first block, instead of the word zone of responsibility, in two places it should say the zone of defence. Thank you. If you recall, we were about to discuss another piece of evidence proffered by the Prosecution on the participation of Dragan Jokic in the reburial operation from paragraph 51 of the indictment. The Prosecution referred to the testimony of Witness P130.
