This is not a witness on the basis of whose testimony any judicial decision should be based, and we have discussed this at length in our closing brief. This witness confirmed during his testimony that as a security officer in the Zvornik Brigade, he played a major role in the process of coordinating the burial activity, the issuing of fuel for this large and secret operation. He was the chief architect of this operation for the Zvornik Brigade. He was given a special vehicle to carry out this task. He was able to reward and punish the participants in this operation. He is a man who is trying to evade his own responsibility and diminish his own role, and therefore, in the statements that he makes to the Prosecution and before the Honourable Trial Chamber, he changed his statement and added new elements to his testimony. And we agree that there is no need to deal with him any further. However, I'm asking you to take into consideration what this Chamber stated in its decision rejecting the motion that this witness be re-examined during the rebuttal case. Let me now go back to paragraph 51 of the indictment. There is no evidence to prove that Dragan Jokic appeared anywhere at the reburial site. Prosecution Witness Richard Butler confirmed that during his many years of investigating this case, he never came across any document that might confirm the participation of the engineers company of the Zvornik Brigade in the reburial operation, and he says so on page 4632 and 4633 of his testimony. Even Dragan Obrenovic, regardless of his animosity towards Jokic, confirmed that he never had any information to the effect that Dragan Jokic participated in the reburial operation. He says on page 2545 to 2546 of his testimony that this is so. And finally Milan Maric, a Defence witness, as confirmed by Mr. Waespi in his closing argument, said that working with Dragan Jokic after the war on Sokolac, when he spoke to him, that is to Dragan Jokic about this operation, he was unable to tell him anything. This is another piece of evidence showing that Dragan Jokic neither took part nor directed the engineers company in this operation. Your Honours, there is no evidence about any other kind of activity on the part of Dragan Jokic, so that this factual allegation from the indictment should also be rejected. Allow me, Your Honours, in this closing argument to refer briefly to paragraph 14 of the indictment, to Dragan Jokic's position as duty officer in the command of the Zvornik Brigade, and the key issue of whether Dragan Jokic had the knowledge required of the final aim of the joint criminal enterprise, whether he knew of the fate of the prisoners brought into the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade in the course of the 14th of July, 1995. According to the Prosecution, he did. He knew, and he assented to this joint criminal enterprise and aided and abetted that enterprise. And as evidence that Dragan Jokic knew about this, the Prosecution uses one, the duty operations officer's notebook P133 and P507, the intercepts of the 14th and 15th of July in which Dragan Jokic allegedly took part. And the third set of evidence are witness statements by witnesses who on the 14th and 15th of July, while Dragan Jokic was duty operations officer, contacted him. There is a list of witnesses there, P130 again, Dragan Obrenovic again, Marko Milosevic, and finally Pero Petrovic. Let us try to go through this evidence again and see the other side of the coin. I do not wish to burden you with the de jure, the normative regulations providing for the duties and tasks of the duty officer. You have heard a lot about this from Mr. Butler, from Mr. Lackovic, from Witness Milan Maric, Ljubo Bojanic, Dusko Vukotic, Momir Nikolic, and so on and so forth. Many of them have spoken about it. (redacted). And I will not go on down the list. The rules regulating what the duty operations officer has to do are before you, Your Honours. This is the instruction on the work of commands and staffs, P394; the rules on the competencies of commands from brigade to regiment level, Defence Exhibit 72/3, the brigade rules, that's P370; the rules of the brigade, P370; and the rules of service in the armed forces. That's Defence Exhibit D71/3. I will refer to these exhibits only briefly. De jure, that is normatively, they prescribe the role of Dragan Jokic as duty operations officer, and there is no need to go through it again. As duty operations officer, he was duty-bound to know what the deployment of the units was in his brigade, to be in contact with his superiors, to be in contact with the units comprising the brigade, to know who his neighbours were to the left and to the right, to make sure that maps are updated, to receive and convey orders. Those were his competencies. We asked Mr. Butler whether the duty operations officer can ever issue commands. His answer was yes, if the commander is absent, if the Chief of Staff is absent, if the assistant commander is absent in the brigade, or if they are not in contact with the brigade. He went on to say when all of these people are absent, then the system begins to fall apart. Mr. Butler was asked whether the duty operations officer, that is Dragan Jokic in that case, could issue orders, and this expert said yes, relying -- well, he said he is duty-bound to receive and pass on orders. Your Honours, this Defence has spent a lot of time on this to point out that Dragan Jokic, as duty operations officer, was not the focus of coordination and communication. Never. From the morning of the 14th to the morning of the 15th when Jokic passed on the duty, never was the brigade without the commander, the Chief of Staff, or the assistant commander. And I think that this is no longer in dispute. Obrenovic himself said, "Yes, I was carrying out the operative command of the brigade until Pandurevic arrived in the afternoon of the 15th of July." If he is not physically present in the command, he is still in charge of radio communications -- or he is still commanding through radio communications - interpreter's apology - and nothing can be done without his approval. We have spent a lot of time showing that in this period he was in the brigade from time to time, and I think we have succeeded in showing this. We say in spite of his guilty plea in which he takes a selective approach to the truth, that Dragan Obrenovic, in the night of the 13th to the 14th of July, was present in the brigade. Look at the testimonies of Milan Maric, Ljubo Bojanovic. They confirm that in the night between the 13th and 14th, he issued orders on the sending of reinforcements to Snagovo, the sending of a unit to Snagovo. On the 14th, in the morning, he was in the brigade command. He called on Jokic to come and be on duty. And the same book of daily orders which we will never try to evade and not for a moment were we afraid to show Dragan Jokic's handwriting there because we want to explain each one of those entries, it shows that Dragan Obrenovic, on the 14th, was in the brigade at one point, and when he wasn't, he operatively was in command and control of the brigade through radio communications. Do you remember Dusko Vukotic, the intelligence officer? He said, "All my intelligence I gave to Dragan Obrenovic. I did not give any information to Dragan Jokic, the duty officer. I wasn't even in communication with him." This is a witness who is a good friend of Dragan Obrenovic, but he told -- told it the way it was. Look at what Milan Maric says. "Obrenovic exerted pressure on me to say that in the night between the 13th and 14th he was at Snagovo with him." And the witness said, "I cannot say that," and his reply was, "Where was I?" And Milan Maric said that after that he did not speak to him again but transferred him to Sokolac. What do these entries in the duty officer's notebook say, P133 and 507? Look at ERN 02935745. There is an entry there, and it says,"Dragan Jokic informed Brano Djuric on the movement of Muslims." I won't read any further. And then it says, "Tomorrow take dry rations. Take old food there." These are all issues that -- these are all orders that Dragan Obrenovic issued. No one else could have issued them. Remember the entry in the afternoon of the 14th? "Reinforcements from the battalion are to be collected and sent to Snagovo to oppose the oncoming column of the 27th division." And Jokic made an entry, "Drive there with Obrenovic's approval." Obrenovic was there, and he was the only one who could say, "Go up there and take up positions at Snagovo." It wasn't the duty operations officer who could do that. That is not our hypothesis. It follows from the intercepts P121, Dekic. And you heard one of those intercepts where Lovac, that's the radio centre, Lovac -- asks Lovac 1, which is Obrenovic's code name, and he admits it, "Are the enforcements on the way?" And Lovac 1, that's Obrenovic, answers, "Yes, they are just starting out." "Where are they starting out from?" "From the command of the Zvornik Brigade, yes." And how does Obrenovic know this? He knows it because he's there. On ERN - I'm speaking of the B/C/S pages - 0235750, again there is an entry by the duty officer, Dragan Jokic. "Premier," that's the radio centre at Gucevo, "-Mumba is asking when Avala is coming to base." Who is Avala? That is Obrenovic's code name. Obrenovic admits it. He arrives at the base and his subordinate Mumba is asking when he is coming. We say at that moment that he was in Orahovac, because that is the only place not covered by the radio signal from Premier, from Gucevo, which is why they lost contact with him at that point. However, time and history will show this. Let's go further. On ERN 02935756 there is an entry at 9.21 hours, that's the morning of the 15th, Your Honours. Obrenovic ordered that reinforcements should urgently be required from the corps. Badem conveyed the order. You know what this is about. And reinforcements arrived from Badem and from the Bratunac Brigade. It is evident that only Obrenovic has operative command, and he is the one issuing the order that reinforcements should be sought from the corps and directed to go to Baljkovica and Parlog, not towards Snagovo. His testimony, Your Honours, is a new virtual reality. He is an intelligent man. He knew exactly how far the Prosecution had come with its evidence, and he limited the facts as far as he was able to do that at that point in time, because the Prosecution had succeeded in discovering his role in these events and then he garnished this with anything that might help him, including involving Jokic in all this. I'm saying "all of this" because of that key sentence that we are dealing with. One of the key pieces of evidence of the Prosecution, that Dragan Jokic knew of the operation of execution and burial is the statement of this same Dragan Obrenovic, who says that on the 15th of July, around 11.00, he met at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, Jokic, that he met Jokic there, and that Jokic as duty officer informed him about the problems with the detention of the prisoners of war and the burial of these prisoners, and that Beara, Popovic, and Drago are doing whatever they want to do and that Popovic told him not to write down any of this. This is an event that was invented or fabricated, Your Honours. Why am I saying this? Allow me to dwell on this a bit longer, if you will. First of all, Obrenovic changes his statement in relation to the place where he met Jokic. Please see his guilty plea in the transcript. He says once it's in the hallway and the other time he says it's on the stairs. You had the opportunity to see this particular site, Your Honours, and I tried to portray both stories objectively. He says that the duty operations officer stopped him on the stairs or in the hall and reported to him about such serious matters. Very compromising matters, that's the way I put it. You've heard quite a bit of evidence. Lackovic, (redacted). There is no reason for anything to be said subjectively about Jokic, who says there is not a single duty officer who in such a place would report to his commander about such things. Such a commander would be no good, and also such a duty officer would be no good. That's what the rules say too. The reporting take place in the premises of the duty officer's room. The regulations and rules say that the duty officer is not allowed to leave his office. But let us assume that that is even the way it did happen, that Jokic went away from the office of the duty officer, and you saw where that was, and that he went downstairs to the left part of the hall of the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. What was he doing there? These premises were not being used at that point in time at all. I showed that to you. There is no denying that. These were the rooms where Vinko Pandurevic's escorts were staying, and at that moment we were returning from Zepa towards Zvornik. Then also there's the military club. That was not being used either. And then the Prosecution says, well, perhaps the toilet was there. Yes, but it was not in order. I saw the toilet -- "I saw and showed them the toilet upstairs." So why would Jokic do that? And then how can the -- how can the major be so brave and so courageous, and how he could speak up in the hallway just like that? Who is he speaking to? And in front of who is he speaking? First of all, to his commander, because that is what Obrenovic is at that time. Secondly, Obrenovic says, "Vasic was going with me." Who is Vasic? A colonel of the police, a man outside the military. And then this same Obrenovic says Vasic could see this, but he was supposed to hear about it, too, because he went on. He went upstairs. What does Vasic say? You received his statement according to Rule 92 bis in which this same Vasic says, "It is true. I was going together with Obrenovic to his office on that day, the 15th, in the morning, but I cannot say that I saw Jokic. I did not see him. I would have said so if I had seen him. I did not hear such a conversation." He says -- in response to a Prosecutor's question, he says, "There is no reason for me not to say that." I am telling you, Your Honours, that this Vasic was much better friends with Obrenovic during the war and after the war than with Jokic. He had nothing to do with Jokic whatsoever. Jokic is a little child as far as he is concerned. He is not at his level, so to speak. If he wanted to say something, he would say something that he could profit from at that point in time, and that is what Obrenovic said, too, because Obrenovic is getting out of the whole story. He made a plea agreement. On the contrary. This witness says, "I did not see Jokic." Obrenovic says, "Behind me are Borovcanin, Stupar, and another officer, I think." We had the opportunity of hearing that Stupar here, and that is what I mentioned in my final brief, that Stupar says, "I did not see Jokic. Had I seen him, I would have said so. And there is no reason for me not to say that I saw him if I did. I only heard of that Jokic when he was building roads in Sekovici." That is the evidence, the key evidence which is supposed to prove that Dragan Jokic was aware of the operation. We can resort to circumstantial evidence as well. Obrenovic says that Jokic said to him that Popovic had ordered him not to write down anything. Your Honours, do you have a shred of evidence to the effect that Popovic was at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade on the morning of the 15th and that he said something like that to Jokic? You do not. There is no evidence that on the 15th in the morning either Popovic or Beara were at the headquarters. And also, the trials against these two persons will show where they were on the morning of the 15th. So on one side we have this virtual reality that is being created by Dragan Obrenovic, and on the other side we have all these facts which state otherwise. It is for you to weigh the two, view them individually, view them together. There are many facts that say the opposite to what Obrenovic said in his admission of guilt. In the entire post-war period, while he was at the position of commander of the 503rd Brigade of the VRS which succeeded the Zvornik Brigade, Obrenovic used all this time to prepare his defence, to revise documents, to conceal documents, and you have all of that in front of you. And he also brought pressure to bear on witnesses so that they would confirm his alibi. His defence concept was that the duty operations officer was the person who had the powers that in reality were exercised by him, Obrenovic himself. All the time he's trying to say that he is in the bushes, that he is in the woods, while three kilometres away from where he says he was people were being killed with his agreement, support, and deep involvement in these events. That is what he says. That is what he admits. And now he is a witness for Dragan Jokic. We will abide by what we said, that in the night in between the 13th and the 14th he's at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade. On the morning of the 14th he leaves the Zvornik Brigade headquarters. The night between the 14th and the 15th, he returns to the brigade. Remember the witnesses with the extraordinary combat reports and also the untruthful thing he said, that he was dictating an extraordinary report from Snagovo. And we had a witness here, Brama Miocevic [phoen], who said this never, ever happened, especially not to an experienced officer like that. He'd never do that kind of thing. He is at brigade headquarters, and that is where he is commanding from. Then the testimony of Mico Gavric, who says, "I came to the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade the night between the 14th and the 15th, and the assistant duty operations officer said to me, "Obrenovic is here. He is asleep." He said that, "You should stay somewhere over here. He has no place to put you up until the morning." Who is Mico Gavric? Why would he speak in favour of Dragan Jokic? He has no idea whatsoever who Dragan Jokic is. And on the morning of the 15th, he left the brigade headquarters and returned again on the 11th. That is the route he took. As days go by and as the Srebrenica investigation progresses, you will see all of this, and you already have quite a bit. So, Your Honours, as regards this kind of witness and this kind of testimony, that cannot be a basis to prove that Dragan Jokic knows about the fate of the prisoners. Again, I wish to reiterate that it is very difficult for any Defence attorney to speak about individual criminal responsibility in the context of tragic events that took place in Srebrenica. I know that best of all, because I come from that part of the world. That is a crime that has no justification. This is a crime that was committed by members of a people that I belong to, too, and I have to feel a sense of obligation in terms of every word I say today, bearing in mind the victims of this crime. However, at the same time I wish to say that the individualisation of the responsibility of each and every participant in this event must be the key and shall be the key of mutual reconciliation and re-establishing a life together in that area. Only a morbid mind could have conceived of this, bringing such a large number of prisoners to Zvornik and executing them. As for what actually happened to the victims, people learned about it after the crime, but this was certainly being concealed before and during the commission of the crime. That is what was said today. This is what the Prosecution said. This was mentioned. And then also this was condemned. There was an outpour of hatred. This could not have been concealed. The Defence cannot say that. But the Defence wishes to say that on that day, the 14th, when Dragan Jokic sees that prisoners are coming to the zone of the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th of July, we're not hiding that, and that is what was said. This was a very long column escorted by UN vehicles, white vehicles in the column. The general story was that they were going to be exchanged. In our final brief we said and enumerated tens of witnesses who said so starting from the victims themselves, via the members of the Bratunac Brigade and the Dutch Battalion, and members of the Zvornik Brigade itself. When the prisoners came, when they were transferred, when they were put up there, all of that that happened is legal and legitimate activity. There is no doubt about that. There is no dilemma involved. This is confirmed by Mr. Butler. There is no war without prisoners. However, taking away the lives of these prisoners is an unprecedented crime. Of course that is quite clear. This was not discussed publicly, because it is quite understandable that those who organised that kind of thing and do such a kind of thing are aware of the fact that they are taking part in a crime. They knew what they were doing, but they're not going to boast about it in public. It is precisely here that the Prosecution tries to say, "This is our proof Dragan Jokic knew what was going on, and he assisted and supported that." They say look at the book of notes of the duty officer. It says there, and I'll state this very briefly, "Salapura called. Drago Beara called Golic." The second note at 1500 hours. "Beara is coming. Orahovac, Petkovci and Rocevic." The third note: "155 Beara should call." And the fourth note: "From Beara, Drago should call." These notes that were written down by Dragan Jokic in the duty officer's book are proof, in the words of the Prosecution, of his participation, because he is informing this other man as to what Beara is doing, and he is assisting him thereby. Who is Beara? As for his position, his character, and his role in these events, Mr. McCloskey spoke about that yesterday, or, rather, the day before yesterday in his closing arguments. This is a high-ranking officer in the Main Staff from the security organs or, to be more precise, the head of administration for security of the Main Staff. It is sure that this kind of officer who is carrying out a criminal design is not going to tell some duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade what he is doing, what his task is, and he is not going to tell him, the duty officer, about what he's doing. He's not duty-bound to report to him. That would have been absurd. That would have been upside down. Dragan Jokic is not at a level that would lead Beara to talk to him. He would not condescend to that. Jokic's duty as duty operations officer in the brigade is to receive and convey information required of him. That is what it says in the rules and regulations. Dragan Jokic cannot go into an analysis of any of these notes. He is not an officer entitled to ask Beara, "why is Drago supposed to call you?" "Beara, why are you looking for Drago?" He is not at that level. He cannot ask Colonel Salapura from the Main Staff why are Drago and Beara supposed to call Golic? In terms of the content of every one of these notes, a priori, it cannot be concluded so pretentiously that Dragan Jokic knows what Beara's work was on the 14th and that he assisted him in carrying out that task because he's writing down these notes. You heard the testimony of Brano Mihic, Salapura, who say, well, he didn't even talk to Jokic. This order or this message was conveyed to the duty officer at the radio centre, and this man took it to the duty officer at the brigade. And then Dragan Jokic, as duty officer, who can he talk to then? How can he say, "Mr. Salapura, why are Drago and Beara supposed to call Golic," who is an intelligence officer at the Drina Corps? He neither asked him nor did he get any answer. It is not his duty to ask him, and he does not dare ask him. That is not evidence. None of these notes prove that Dragan Jokic knows about the executions. At every point in time, this Defence was prepared to say to the honourable Prosecution that any one of these notes can be commented upon. We had nothing to shy away from in this respect. The other group of these questions are the intercepts, the intercepts, the four intercepted conversations at 9.10 on the 14th, allegedly Jokic and Zivanovic. There was another intercept at 2102 between Jokic and Zivanovic. At 2110, there were several participants, Beara, Jokic. And the fourth conversation at 2120, a conversation between Jokic and Vilotic. Vilotic, one assumes, might in actual fact have been General Miletic. During this trial, for the sake of principle, we did not shy away from these intercepts in as far as they were incriminating, but we did say that a ruling and a judgement cannot be based on such intercepts. However, we do take into account the fact that the Honourable Trial Chamber has decided to admit these into evidence and then attribute their relevant weight to them at the end. But Your Honours, there is no recording of these intercepts. The people who listened in to these conversations, intercepted these conversations, claim that they encountered problems and that errors were made when the tapes were switched and that the tapes on the Uher recorder were four hours long, that the timer was out of order, so that errors were made as far as the timing on the -- of the intercepts, and these errors could -- could have a bearing on the identity of the participants in these conversations. When asked while listening from Konjekeroke Visnjica [phoen], how can you know who the persons are who are talking at a distance about 80 kilometres away from you? And most of them said we identified frequent participants in these conversations by the sound, but Dragan Jokic's voice was not recognised by or identified by anyone, because he was not a frequent participant. Pavle Zivanovic, Krstic, Vasic, Obrenovic, yes, those voices were identified. Well, then, how do you know that Jokic took part in these conversations? And then he says, well, he identifies himself. And perhaps he introduces himself as the duty operations officer. This is a good opportunity to remind you, Your Honours, that in the Zvornik Brigade at that point in time, on the 14th and 15th of July, as well as before and after those days, and this is not disputed, there is a duty operations officer at the forward command post, too, and he is the centre point for coordinating all communications. We have heard Witness Lackovic and Witness Vukotic on this point. Why is the centre point there at the forward command post? Well, he says simply because the commander is based there. That is where the orders are coming from. That is where the commands are coming from. There was a lot of fighting going on. The column of the 28th Division was on its way through. There was a major breakthrough that was under way. The 2nd Corps of the BH army was about to overrun the area. As for the intercepts, the radio communication on that day was a chaos. This all shows that we should approach with a great deal of caution any statements indicating that Jokic took part in those conversations. We addressed each and every one of these intercepts separately in our final brief. Therefore, I don't think there's any need to dwell on this any longer. We abide by the theory that we put forward in our final brief in relation to these intercepts, but for the sake of history, at this point in time, if we look at those four intercepts, what is it in there that constitutes proof that Dragan Jokic was aware of the executions that were going on? The Prosecutor says, well, he was aware where the combat situation on the ground. He was talking to Zivanovic. He knew about the deployment of the forces, he was well-informed. Well, what can I say? Well, yes, he was. That is a duty of the duty operations officer. There is no escaping that. But does it follow from that that he actually knew about the killings? There are two conversations, two intercepts that contain references to someone who is alleged to be Jokic as saying, "We have problems with the prisoners," that is the parcels, and this has been used many times throughout the trial. But, Your Honours, I'm never going to even try to imply that Dragan Jokic was not aware of the prisoners being there. That would be insane. It would be an insane line of reasoning to pursue. But who in their right state of mind could presume that he was evil enough to assume that those people would be killed? We have no proof of that, and this is the essence of what we are saying. This is the essence of what we have to say in relation to these intercepts. Finally, I will refer to an intercept that Mr. Waespi referred to two days ago. It is the morning of the 15th. There is an intercept of a conversation between Pandurevic, Jokic, Milosevic, and Mijatovic. Pandurevic is calling, saying, "I want to speak to the duty operations officer." Therefore, he's calling the centre. The duty operations officer answers the phone. Major Jokic speaking. And as soon as Pandurevic realises it's Major Jokic who is on the line, he asks to speak to Mijatovic. "I don't even want to talk to you," he says. Allegedly Jokic answers, "just a moment, commander," and then Mijatovic comes in. And then he reports to his zone commander on the situation in the brigade because at that moment, the commander is on his way from Zepa to Zvornik to assist with the breakthrough across the front lines that is being carried out by the forces of the 28th Division at that time. I do not wish to be applying a double standard here in relation to these transcripts. Please don't get me wrong. But if we properly evaluate these intercepts, if we evaluate precisely what they actually say, who is Dragan Jokic in his capacity of duty operations officer? Well, even this commander refuses to even speak to him. He says, "I want to speak to Mijatovic." Who is Mijatovic? We heard about this, Your Honours. He is a logistics officer. He is Pandurevic's confidence man. Jokic is there, present, alive and well. He is duty operations officer. Purportedly he should be the centre point of all communications. He knows about everything, he aided everything and abetted everything, and here we see him swept away by Pandurevic. "You get out of the way. Let me speak to Mijatovic so I an know what is going on at the brigade." So what better illustration can there be about what his actual role and position was. Therefore, please don't get me wrong on this. I do not wish to fall into the trap of, on the one hand, using the transcripts in my own favour and rejecting them elsewhere. We are just trying to get them evaluated in truthful light, to get them evaluated properly as they deserve to be viewed. And then the third set of evidence of the Prosecutor claiming that Dragan Jokic knew of the executions that were under way and that he aided and abetted those executions. They say Witness Pero Petrovic said that he had talked to Jokic and that Jokic had told him, well, yes, there are prisoners of war arriving in Pilica, but that's nothing for you to worry about, so just go home. Your Honours, we have provided sufficient evidence showing that Pero Petrovic is simply not telling the truth. We have also brought over Zoran Radosavljevic who testified exactly the opposite to what Pero Petrovic said. We have provided material evidence that he was, in fact, not telling the truth. I'm talking about the Republika Srpska telecom certificate which explicitly states that the phone lines from Pilica were fully operational on that day where he comes up with a story that the phone lines were down and that's why he had to go to a different location four kilometres away and use the phone there. This witness is not even sure that he talked to Dragan Jokic at all. He says, "I spoke to the duty operations officer, and I think it was Jokic." This witness is not sure about the date either. He said it was on the 12th of July, St. Peter's Day. That is simply not true. It could have been on the 14th of July, for example, because that's when Dragan Jokic was on duty. If you look at the testimony of that witness, nothing can be based on that. His testimony is an attempt to divert the Prosecutor's attention from his own responsibility, because the premises of the Pilica local commune, as you have seen for yourselves, Your Honours, of which he was president had been used to keep prisoners, and he was the one who held the keys to those premises, not someone else like he wishes to have us believe. Likewise, this also happened back in 1992, when a set of tragic events occurred there as testified to by Witness DV1 before this Trial Chamber. And then we find out that he knows nothing. He simply goes back home because Jokic tells him these are prisoners of war, feel free to go home. And Zoran Radosavljevic, a witness, says he is lying, for God's sake. He came with me to see the prisoners. No ruling can be based on a statement given by a witness like this. Again, Your Honour -- Your Honours, even if he had said "these are prisoners of war, go home," does that prove that they would be killed? Let us not even remind ourselves. What if he said, for example, "I know nothing of the prisoners"? This is also in reference to Marko Milosevic's testimony, which was also addressed by the OTP. He was the deputy commander of the 6th Battalion, Your Honour. The OTP knows and states clearly in their indictment, in the zone of defence of the 6th Battalion, that is in Petkovci, crimes were committed. The OTP claims that members of the 6th Battalion were involved in guarding the prisoners, transporting the prisoners, and removing the bodies of the prisoners who had been killed in that school that we visited, Your Honours. And this witness is a deputy commander of that specific battalion. So what does he tell us? He says on the 14th I received a phone call from the duty operations officer from the brigade. It was in the morning. And he said that prisoners would be arriving in the school building. Which duty operations officer was this? I don't know. "Frankly, I don't know that this was Dragan Jokic." He did say that before this Chamber. And indeed the prisoners arrived. He went to the front line and he was wounded there, so he was taken to a hospital. Three days later, he learns from someone that people who were 500 metres from his command post had been killed. Come on. This is simply not a story that anyone in their right state of mind could possibly believe. There is only one detail that we must extract from all this evidence. He was asked by the OTP, "why is the duty operations officer calling you? Why wasn't he calling the commander? You are the deputy commander." And he says, "Well, my commander was away at that time because he had taken some soldiers over to the Zvornik Brigade command so that they could go to Snagovo with Obrenovic." If we look at the duty operations logbook P133 it clearly reflects that his commander, Ostoja Stanisic, did indeed bring soldiers to the command of the Zvornik Brigade at that time. Try to imagine now, Your Honours, Jokic is there sitting in the Zvornik Brigade command, and there before him is the commander of the battalion. He is supposed to tell him what the prisoners were there for but that's not what he does. He picks up the phone and he calls his deputy who at the time is in Petkovci. Why on earth would he do anything like that? Why don't you just tell the commander? He's there. Send this message on by courier. Again we have another story which is merely an attempt to avoid the truth of what really happened at Petkovci. It's easy to blame Dragan Jokic. Even as early as his first statement, the first statement that he gave back to the Prosecutor back in Zvornik, he was a lamb for the slaughter, and he was the black sheep, someone to be blamed, the scapegoat. I'm not sure I should go on about this. To put it briefly, he said on the 14th he called the duty operations officer so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would very much like that statement to be in evidence. If counsel would like it to be in evidence at this stage it might be enlightening, but I know the Court's rulings have not allowed it into evidence, and I think that's what we must go on unless counsel wishes to change their position, which perhaps they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And another matter, Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- we are three hours and a half at this moment. How many pages left from those pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Four pages to go, Your Honours. I'll try to be as quick as I can. I'm about to bring it to an end. But please allow me. My apologies. I am not using P130, this statement that was not admitted. I am actually referring to evidence that he gave before this Trial Chamber. I'm not dealing with him any more because we are in agreement that this is not a credible witness. He said, "I called him on the phone, and I talked to the duty operations officer asking for assistance in guarding the prisoners." He did say that to this Trial Chamber under oath. He said, "I wasn't sure whether the duty operations officer was Jokic, but when the investigator told me it was Jokic, it was then that I remembered, yes, Jokic was the person that I had spoken to." An hour later, he says, Sreten Milosevic, Branko Jovanovic, and some other people from the logistics unit, they came to guard the prisoners. The unfortunate Tanacko Tanic was also one of them, a witness that was here in front of you, who clearly stated, "Jokic never sent me there. Jokic was in no position to give me orders. I was sent there by Mijatovic. I saw Witness P130 there but I never saw Jokic." How can this be testimony to the effect that Dragan Jokic aided and abetted the execution of prisoners there? Well, Your Honours, it's up to you to decide that. This brings me to the end of my story on the all the evidence you have heard over the last one and a half years as it concerned the knowledge of Dragan Jokic, his knowledge of these executions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stojanovic. I had misunderstood the previous objection. I thought he was talking about the statement of his client. He was not as I read this over again. So I should have withdrawn that, and I have no problem with him discussing Witness 130. That's -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the sake of history and because I am returning to Eastern Bosnia tomorrow, I have to say this: It is very difficult for me to explain this idea of a joint criminal enterprise as it is used here. It is hard to explain that Dragan Jokic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise because he was to have foreseen the intentions in the minds of a group of people he did not belong to. Your Honours, Dragan Jokic could not have foreseen the consequences. As he told me yesterday, it is not clear to him to this day. He asked me yesterday why is Mr. Waespi talking to me about Bratunac, about the 13th, about looking for an excavator? What have I to do with that? And yet he is charged with all the opportunistic killings that took place in Bratunac before the 14th and the opportunistic killings in the Zvornik Brigade after the 14th, because he is supposedly a member of the joint criminal enterprise who aided and abetted all this. It is hard for me to say this, but you had a witness before you, Your Honours, who pleaded guilty for the events in 1992 and fabricated a virtual reality about Srebrenica in 1995, who said that he talked to Karadzic on the 7th, 8th, or 9th about how all these people should be killed. He said that on the night of the 13th he said, "Take these prisoners away from here. Don't kill them in Zvornik." How he opposed this. How on the 17th taking a vehicle and members of the DutchBat he signed a statement saying that everything had been done in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. And yet this man is not said to be a member of the joint criminal enterprise in Srebrenica. He could not have foreseen what would happened, and Dragan Jokic could have? His story, his role and the role of Dragan Jokic in the events in Srebrenica, Your Honours, this is a night and day difference in Eastern Bosnia. This is something I can never explain. There had to be intent to aid and abet a crime. There had to be intent. And, Your Honours, Dragan Jokic did not have this intent. This is the evidence that both the Prosecution and I have discussed, and it is up to you to make a decision on it. Let me now just speak briefly about the following: Should Your Honours find that Dragan Jokic is guilty, that he is a war criminal, I wish to put forward the mitigating circumstances in his favour. Dragan Jokic is a man who had a typical career in the former socialist Yugoslavia. He came from a poor family. And because military training was free, he went to the military academy. He chose the engineers because the training was shorter, and he thought he would start earning his living sooner if he chose that. And secondly, he would not be carrying weapons but using machines to build roads and other facilities and help people. This was his choice. When the war broke out, he had to respond to the call to return to his native town. On his arrival he worked as a teacher in the Divic training centre for young soldiers based in the hotel Vidikovac. After the establishing of the engineering company and the successful work on fortifying the zone of defence of the Zvornik Brigade and directing obstacles around it, Jokic was offered the duty of brigade commander. However, he was aware of the responsibility this duty carried with it, as well as the bloodshed that had already happened in April and May 1992, and for this reason he refused to take up this duty. When plans were being made to attack the Srebrenica subregion in 1992, Jokic refused to take part in these operations. After this, he was dismissed from the duty of Chief of Staff by this same general Zivanovic, and Captain Dragan Obrenovic was appointed in his place. From that point, the attitude toward Dragan Jokic changed. Zivanovic instructed Pandurevic and Obrenovic to exclude Jokic from any sort of decision-making because there was no place for those who were disobedient in the chain of command. Throughout the war, Jokic fought against the negative phenomena occurring in his environment. He fought against the looting of Muslim property. He fought against paramilitary formations, for which reason his personal safety and the safety of his family was under threat. Witness P178, and I have been told I may say his name, Ostoja Stanojevic, said at one point that he had a pure soul and a heart of gold, and these are words which characterise Dragan Jokic best. Another witness referred to him as Nikoletina Bursac, a character from Serbian literature from World War II, a good natured, large man with a soft heart, a heart that was belied by his appearance, his outward appearance. And this is the image of Dragan Jokic. We have spoke a lot about the evidence that on the 18th of July when the worst crimes were taking place, he made a personal sacrifice, and he let a group of Muslim young men walk through a minefield, and this is not the action of an evil man. It is not characteristic of those who actually were members of the joint criminal enterprise. When the war was over, Your Honours, after the Prosecution called on him the first time, he responded to the call. On the 14th of December, 1990, he made a statement to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1999, interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he told them everything he knew. After that he was treated very badly and harassed. He was said to be a traitor. He was insulted. He was subject to threats. His family was exposed to threats. Again, on the 2nd of April, 2000, he was asked to speak to the Prosecution, and in the second interview he started being evasive, saying that he could not remember. And when the Prosecution insisted that he say what happened, he stopped. And then he was told he would be indicted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. First of all, that's not true. Secondly, now we are getting into the statements. So I was wrong before, but I think I'm pretty clearly right this time, as befuddled as my brain appears to be becoming. So again, I make that offer. If those -- if he would like those statements in evidence, it's not too late, and we're ready to accept them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, please concentrate on those mitigating factors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I accept this suggestion, and I will conclude by saying that after he was told that he had been indicted and after his then-counsel conveyed this message to him, he responded again. He said, "Here I am. I surrender. There is no where for me to flee. I have said everything I had to say. You can try me. I am not guilty." He is the only officer of the army of Republika Srpska, Your Honours, from then to this day who did that, who surrender voluntarily, who said, "Here I am." And that is how he has acted from the beginning to today. The Court appreciated this and gave him provisional release. He respected every summons. He respected all the conditions imposed on him. Not for a moment did he try to obstruct the course of justice. His behaviour in the Detention Unit, his behaviour after the execution of the crime, if you should find that he was guilty of that, was that he whole-heartedly worked on the implementation of the Dayton Accords. He participated in the de-mining of hundreds of thousands of square kilometres of land making it fit for agriculture. And all this demonstrates that he is not an evil man. He is not a man who could have done something like that. Let us hear the words of Witness DV1, who is certainly competent to evaluate Dragan Jokic's position. He said that after talking to many contemporaries of the events in Zvornik, because he is writing a book about it and he was involved in these events himself directly, he said that out of hundreds of testimonies, he heard only one, and that all this shows that Dragan Jokic did not participate in these events. This witness confirms that he himself knew what Dragan Jokic went through after he made his first statement. Mirko Rebic, a witness who grew up together with Jokic and who had a high-ranking position in Zvornik municipality said that he, Mirko Rebic is a religious man and that God is his witness that he is telling the truth when he says that he thinks Dragan Jokic is a good man and that he was not involved in any crimes. I will now conclude, Your Honours. The first victim in any war is the truth. Your Honours, it is up to you to establish what is most difficult in this case, and that is the truth about these tragic events and the truth about the role of Dragan Jokic in all these events. I am deeply convinced that you will successfully carry out your historic mission and that you will evaluate all this evidence properly and that we shall all be the winners because we will all gain the truth about these events. Taking into account everything said both by the Prosecution and the Defence, all the evidence you have seen, please also bear in mind the character of Dragan Jokic, his personality and everything that in this past year and a half you were able to hear and learn about him. On behalf of this Defence, I wish to thank you for your most proper conduct of these proceedings and for being so fair and so lenient with us. Let me reiterate, Your Honours, that I ask you to acquit Dragan Jokic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's time for us to have our break, and we will resume at 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.48 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] We move that the exhibit - I mean D77/3 - be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
