utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. No objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This document is admitted into the evidence. Thank you. Well, Mr. McCloskey, are you ready or do you have any rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I -- yes, Mr. President, I -- I have rebuttal. I will hopefully be brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But before I -- I get to that, I wanted to just take a moment to thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours, for what has been now over a year and a half of your very, very careful attention to this case. It has been much appreciated as has the fairness by which you have treated all the parties and I think everyone shares my view on that, and by which the great patience and grace by which you carried out your duties, which unfortunately I can't say I always met my own expectations in that matter. In fact, last night I had words that should have been unsaid and had no place for this Tribunal. I know you have made a great effort to have this courtroom a -- the kind of a place that would stand as an example for international justice, and I apologise that I -- I said words that did not belong here. You have seen us all for a year and a half. You know us in some ways better than we know ourselves, our temperaments, our flash points and our characters, and I know you go about your deliberations very carefully. So let me just briefly respond, first, if I could, to the arguments of counsel for Jokic. First of all, I want to clarify that it's not the position of the Prosecutor that Mr. Jokic should be held responsible for the incidents that occurred in the area of Bratunac, and it is -- there are some cases and under the joint criminal enterprise where perhaps this is appropriate. It is not my viewpoint that in this case it is. I want you to begin looking at this case seriously regarding Mr. Jokic on the morning of the 14th of July when he takes over as duty officer. In addition, the indictment has mentioned factually that Mr. Jokic directed one of the soldiers in the burial -- or the burial -- or the retrieval of bodies at Kravica. It is not -- it is my position that the Prosecution has not proven beyond a reasonable doubt that he had knowledge that he was sending that person to Kravica. I think the evidence was that on the morning of the 14th of July, there was a lot of bodies and -- in Bratunac, and that there was -- certainly Major Jokic directed and ordered his, at that point, subordinate down there to help out with that, but I'm not satisfied that there is sufficient evidence to tie him into the actual Kravica warehouse situation. I would also like to clarify what I have clarified before, that we are not charging Mr. Jokic as a commander either through the front door or the back door, and you've heard my explanations for that over and over again, and I won't -- I won't go into them. And most of our argument was, I think, covered by the brief and by Mr. Waespi, so I will -- won't spend much time at all, but I do want to take up on a theme that Mr. Stojanovic left with us, where he acknowledged that on the 14th of July, Major Jokic had knowledge of the prisoners in the schools. This means that Mr. Jokic knew that there were thousands of prisoners at Orahovac school, at Petkovci school, Rocevic, Kula, as we have argued, where they had no business being. This is in no way, shape or form a weigh station to prison or anywhere else, many of which were these little guys with their berets, or their younger kids, no food, no water. And on the 14th of July, Mr. Jokic ordered one of his people to go to Orahovac where he knew there were thousands of prisoners to go with an excavator. An excavator is not a bulldozer. A bulldozer is a big scraping thing that flattens and builds roads. An excavator dig holes. No other reason in the world to send an excavator to Orahovac than to dig graves. You've heard Major Jokic is from Grbavci. This is the area. You've heard everybody knew what was going on there. And I just wanted to clear up one point. Exhibit 507, where there is a brief reference about a message to Major Jokic about a dump truck and a loader. Mr. Stojanovic mentioned that that was -- message was passed on in the future tense, that it should be conveyed to Jokic. The official translation that I have says, "At 2210 hours, the first battalion asked for one loader, one excavator and a dump truck with a tarpaulin to be at Pilica at 0800 hours, conveyed to Jokic and Milosevic." That's the official translation that we have. And finally, we know that Mr. Jokic ordered one of his men to Kozluk on the 16th with an excavator. And we know that by the 16th of July roughly a thousand men had been killed and buried at Orahovac, roughly a thousand men had been killed and buried at Petkovci. Somewhere between 500 and a thousand men have been killed and -- at Kozluk. So somewhere between 3 to 4.000 men are dead, lying dead within a few kilometres of the engineering compound when Major Jokic orders his man to take an excavator to Kozluk. The evidence in this case is clear. Mr. Stojanovic went through it, made his arguments. You will see our arguments. I'm sure you will find beyond a reasonable doubt that he is guilty as we have charged. Now, let me turn to the case against Colonel Blagojevic. I just want to remind the Court of a few things. One, counsel for Blagojevic spoke of the Karremans-Mladic meeting issue. One -- one fact that cannot be left out, it's -- in evaluating that material is it comes in from Major Franken, who on the 11th of July stated the VRS spoke to them on the radio, I believe, and this was at a time when there were many Dutch soldiers in the custody of the VRS as hostages, and the VRS said, threaten them, that if they -- if NATO got involved or if there was anything like that, they would kill the hostages. So when you're looking at DutchBat and Mladic and evaluating the situation there, don't forget that historical fact. The Defence also asked you to take great weight on the credibility of witness Mico Gavric when he testified that Colonel Blagojevic told him to look after the prisoners, but we agree with Mr. Karnavas that it is your job to determine what is reasonable and what is not, and if there are two reasonable explanations, you should accept the explanation of the Defence. We're not -- we do not shy away from that, because it's clear what is reasonable. And let me just make -- remind you briefly of Mico Gavric, and you will see that it is completely unreasonable to accept him as a truthful witness on that point. Mico Gavric said in a question asked about whether or not there had been any shelling in Srebrenica, and he said, "The Bratunac Brigade, I'm talking about the Bratunac artillery battery, in fact did not fire in the direction of the enclave until the 11th of July, 1995." Well, having heard that comment, we found a document which is Exhibit 856, and I'll just show it to you briefly. It was Colonel Blagojevic's, as far as we know, first interim combat report where he in the first paragraph said, "Pursuant to Colonel Lazic's verbal order we fired two times two projectiles from howitzer 105 millimetre on Srebrenica town. Projectiles were fired at 1907 hours." So clearly the colonel is acknowledging he took these orders. And 105-millimetre howitzer on the town of Srebrenica is a very ugly thing to do. That's why I said on May 24th I wanted to give him credit. I don't know if this war got to him like it did others, but on May 25th, he gets no credit for following this order. Also, there's been some issue about Pribicevac. Just look at the next line: "Artillery observers from Pribicevac reported that two projectiles fell in the vicinity of the Domavija building. Other two projectiles were not observed." Well, we know that from the little house at this village from Pribicevac and from Kula hill that you can't see Pribicevac and witnesses testified to that and that was confirmed, but we've also learned that places like Snagovo are also areas, so I think this can be cleared up by Pribicevac is referred to as probably an area in this particular message. And as you saw, there were some heights above Pribicevac that were likely an artillery sighting spot. I don't think it's a hugely relevant point as to -- I think it's good to clear it up so that you can see that. Also, Mica Gavric, if you recall, he was the one that was ordered by Blagojevic to search the terrain on the 17th, and he acknowledged that four children, four boys, were separated from the group. Of course, it's our view that that was the continuing operation to separate the young men, and this was a reflection of that continuing operation. And Mico Gavric said there were 35 prisoners. I think it was Dusko Jevic said there were 200. Why would Mico Gavric underestimate the number of prisoners? We have no evidence of what happened to those 200. Mico Gavric is not someone to trust when it comes to caring for prisoners. The document that came out under the hand of -- excuse me, not the hand but the name of Colonel Blagojevic, 501, talked about this incident and said, "Among the Muslim prisoners, there are four underaged children between 8 and 14 who are being held in the military custody in Bratunac. One of them told the commander of the unit that was searching the area about a large number of Muslim troops committing suicide or killing each other. We propose that this testimony be recorded by cameras for your press centre." This is clearly using children as propaganda to provide an explanation why Muslims are dying. Why do you do that on the 17th of September -- excuse me, 17th of July? Is this a newsworthy event by itself that Muslims are committing suicide? I don't think it's any kind of a defence unless you're worried about it. Counsel for Blagojevic also ask you to look at Exhibit 480, which is a 13 July document by Radoslav Jankovic, colonel from the Main Staff. He argued that this document showed that Jankovic was not aware of the murder operation. Well, please look carefully at that document. I won't take the time to read it all now to you, but I can't see that in any reasonable interpretation that I see. He first talks about noting the various patients that are in custody of -- of UNPROFOR and in their care, and the doctors of UNPROFOR, people that as far as we know all survived, and he talks about the doctor that -- or watching those patients. And he says in the first paragraph, "I intend to send him away tomorrow under the pretext that his help is not necessary." Well, we know what the "under the pretext" means. He means he's going to lie to this guy to get rid of him. Why do you need to do that? Why not keep these doctors around to help care for people? It doesn't show that this is a document of goodwill and lack of knowledge. And then in the last paragraph he has a PS: "I think that if we want to take over the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde in the same way, it will be necessary to present the operation in Srebrenica in the media so as to show that we had rendered adequate treatment to civilians and even to soldiers who surrendered their weapons." This is a man that shared an office with Momir Nikolic, that was one of perhaps three Main Staff officers that was present throughout the entire time period. This is propaganda he's talking about. It's nothing more than propaganda. Setting it up. If we're going to take Zepa, we need to do it and present it to the world like we did it right. The world knew, as you heard, within days that Srebrenica was not done correctly. There is document that I -- as I was reviewing the argument that is an interesting document that we put into evidence on that subject. It's one of Dragomir Vasic's reports from the 12 July. He writes to his superiors that Mladic is not -- is going -- something to the effect he hasn't yet decided to do with the Muslim men. So from that document, it appears that Vasic has not yet been allowed in on the plan to kill the Muslim men, but it is not a document that suggests that there is not a plan to kill Muslim men. But take a look at that document. That is the one document that talks about this issue, shows that Mladic has this fixation with the men. He's not telling Vasic it was probably one of these meetings with civilian people present. He is not telling him what he had in mind for the Muslim men. That is on the 12th of July. I believe it is before they start getting separated and treated like animals. Mr. Karnavas said in an argument that you have no shelling of civilians. Now, you saw perhaps both Mr. Karnavas and myself, especially at one hour and 15 minutes we got a little excited at times. I don't know if this is one of those times, but I need to respond to it. Of course we saw shelling. The UNMO reports Kingori, he spoke of Kingori and the Defence view of Kingori but the DutchBat reports the Muslim civilians. Remember, if you can, the -- I think it was Boering, it may have been his colleague, they went to Srebrenica on the 10th to meet with the -- with the Muslim army there, and there was a lot of people surrounding the base. You saw pictures of the crowd, and they -- testimony came in about a shell that landed amongst the crowd, right in front of them, and wounded people is my recollection. Mr. Karnavas also argued and -- that Momir Nikolic was a self-manager. I address you to that argument because to have any kind of a self-manager in a military organisation is absolutely absurd. Self-managers in the military become front-line fodder. They are not allowed to self-manage themselves. Now, some officers give people authority, pass on that -- their authority, though they retain the responsibility, and it appears that Momir Nikolic was given the job to be the liaison officer. He had a nice corner office. But we don't see any evidence that he is somehow outside this organisation. This is so fundamentally contrary, especially for an army of the JNA which was very discipline oriented. It did not have the -- the discretionary rules that some of the more -- the other western armies were developing at the time. This is a tough army. People were not allowed to run amok. And he'd been in that brigade for a long time. The other thing I'd ask you on that point is what evidence is there that there was any problems between Momir Nikolic and Colonel Blagojevic? There really -- Mr. Karnavas mentioned something that Nikolic said, but I don't recall any evidence that there were significant problems. We can easily recall the issues that were going on up in Zvornik between Drago Nikolic and Pandurevic and Obrenovic where it was the -- you know, the issues of the security guy that didn't want to be -- have to do duty officer. He wanted his reports to be secret and, you know, he had his own car, and these sort of competing issues that are a result of the -- the way security worked and the establishment of the counter-intelligence wing of that, and so we saw that there was tension. Of course, despite that tension, what's the first thing Drago Nikolic do but call his commander. So I don't see a problem. And we had all these officers that testified, and no one talks about a problem with Momir Nikolic. Some of them don't like him, but we don't see an issue that there's a problem between the two. The other thing that is just fundamentally not reasonable, and sometimes you forget because we've heard it so long, a commander can't just say suddenly, "I don't have my intel and security officer. I can't just tell you my left arm is gone." That makes no military sense. Now, just because he is his commander doesn't mean he's guilty by definition. That's not what I'm saying. But I think it's very important for you to realise that. Popovic, no. Nikolic, no. It doesn't work that way. Mr. Karnavas also said that Momir Nikolic did not coordinate any units. And let me read you what Assistant Commander Trisic said on that point. And this was a question from Mr. Karnavas: "All right. Now I want to fast forward to July 12th, 13th and so on. During that period of time can Captain Nikolic tell you that he had been appointed the coordinator of the units that were in Potocari at that time? No, he didn't tell me. When you were there did you see him by any chance coordinating among the various units? Well, he was there and he was doing the work and that is it, coordination." And then it goes off to other subjects. I also want to briefly point out - I'm told my time is about up and I think we should take care of that, I'm almost through - that he states that Colonel Blagojevic is a man of no importance, just like Nikolic, although Nikolic wants to be a man of importance, hence why he's a guest at the UN Detention Unit. I don't know what that means. And then counsel argues, but you don't see anybody reporting to Blagojevic. Well, I want to take you back to the testimony, and I won't -- but I -- of Dragomir Zekic. I believe he was the commander of the 3rd Battalion. He told Ms. Issa in testimony that he reported to Colonel Blagojevic personally on the 11th and the 17th, and via communications on the 12th, 13th, 14th, and 15th, and 16th. It's very clear from the testimony. You'll see that. And Trisic, assistant -- the assistant commander for rear services, in an interview by Dean Manning, said that first he reported his dealings with the logistics of the operational 12th and 13th to the corps, and then he said, "After that, my commander, of course." I read that back to him, if you recall, and I asked him, "Do you stand by that statement?" And he said, "Yes, I do." So at that point, clearly we have people reporting to Blagojevic. We also have the witness who was a protected witness, but he was the senior officer that was -- was with Colonel Blagojevic on each of the important days, and he again describes to Ms. Issa how when they came back together on the 11th, they did what a commander and assistant should do. They reviewed the various documents and reports and familiarised themselves with what's going on in the brigade. On the 11th. He said the same thing on the 12th, the same thing on the 13th. And he says he's -- Blagojevic is with him at the time. So you've got people reporting to him. You've got him there on those evenings checking the records like he should, checking with people like he should, and we know what was going on during that time frame. Mr. Karnavas also asked you to look carefully and take credence in the witness of Keserovic, a security officer. And I want just briefly to read you about Keserovic, because I want you to do the same thing. It's asked: "I want to ask you if this example I'm giving you is an internal threat to the security of a unit. If prisoners within the custody of an army are systematically abused by the people guarding them, can that threaten the safety and security of that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a public matter. That does not fall under counter-intelligence information in the sense in which I mentioned it or in the sense in which it is treated by the rules of service and relevant laws. This is something that has to do with order, discipline, responsibility, something that may constitute a threat in relation to the general security of the unit, but it cannot fall into the category of secret counter-intelligence information. One's superior officer always has to be aware of such information. That is to say the commanding officer of the unit and also the person higher up in the chain of command. Everybody has to be informed about this, and everybody has to take measures with a view to resolving the problem, but it's a public matter, so to speak." Mr. Karnavas also told you that the MPs didn't know anything. Well, look at the testimony of the protected witness that was a high-ranking officer in that unit and what other witnesses said about him and where he was, what he was doing. He was in Bratunac the night of the 13th trying to get people to help his people guard the Muslim men. Look at the testimony of MP Nikola Popovic. He and others are assigned to guard the Muslims inside the school on the night of the 13th. Mile Janjic, he's also guarding prisoners the night of the 13th and 14th, around vehicles. Borivoje Jakovljevic, another MP. He's guarding people around the Vuk Karadzic school. Slobodan Mijatovic, he also guarded people at the school. And they tell various versions of what they see and what they hear. But when you look at them, remember, and this can be difficult because many of these people were 92 bis, but the survivors, there were really eight that have to do with Bratunac and the Kravica Supermarket. Five were in vehicles. Four of those were around Bratunac, one in front of Kravica, three were in schools. What they say is remarkably consistent, and it is horrendous Mr. Karnavas also said that nothing happened until the 13th. Well, don't forget the testimony, it's 92 bis Witness P110. He's an old guy, testified at the Krstic trial. He got separated from Potocari on the 12th and got put into Bratunac on the 12th and put into one of these buildings, and he gets asked this question: "Q. Now could you tell us the Judges your experience that you had and what was observed happening to the other Muslim men who were in that room that particular night and the early morning hours that followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we entered, there wasn't enough room and we complained that we could -- we would suffocate, and then the Serb soldiers shot over our heads and shouted, keep silent or we'll kill you all. And then we fell silent. And someone in the area where we had entered said you 12 have to carry out the assignment given to you. Do you understand that? He was speaking in a sharp tone. And then a group said yes, sir to one. And then Serb soldiers came with flashlights and they lighted us up. And then they ask where people were from. The people from Glogova, people from Cerska, people from Bratunac, and people answered. And then they said the people from Glogova, get up. One man got up. The Serb soldier said, come out here. He left the warehouse to the left, the direction through which we had entered the warehouse. We could hear blunt blows and his screams and moans. When all this stopped again they came back with their flashlights and calling out people from various places. Nobody admitted to being from those places, so then the flashlight was pointed at random." He goes on to describe how people got taken out and they hear shots, and sometimes they bring them back in and throw half dead or dead bodies onto the crowd and people have to carry bodies out. He also says that the night of the 13th he's gets transported up to the area around Zvornik which he knows is near Karakaj, and this is something else that the counsel has contested. This was the first trip up to the area of Zvornik. This survivor says so. It's corroborated by Dragan Obrenovic and Witness 130, and the records related to the IKM forward command post. There's also a record at about 1.00 a.m., I believe. It's a food record from the Zvornik food service showing that food was delivered to the MPs at Orahovac at about 1.00 on the 14th. So there's no question that this operation was fully under way by that time. And I don't think I need to go into my further arguments on those points. So those were the points I wanted to make, and we're at the end of a very long road, and again I just want to give you my thanks and turn the case over to my -- my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, do you have any rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the first time in 20 years that I have the opportunity, because where I come, we don't get this opportunity. So I'm looking forward to it. But I will be short. I'm just going to hit the points. With Mr. Gavric, again what we see is the Prosecution doing what I call the a-la-carte approach to the facts, taking what they like, leaving the rest. Mr. Gavric, when he was testifying, apparently did not remember the May 25th incident. It was brought to his attention during cross-examination. He was shown the document, and then he indicated that he recollected. In fact, if you go back to the submissions of the Prosecution in their motion to reopen their case, just by coincidence they had mentioned that. And again we saw that they mention one page, and then if you went to the following page you saw where you got the full understanding of Mr. Gavric's position. So I think you need to look at all of the testimony of Mr. Gavric before you -- you reach a conclusion as to whether he was being truthful or untruthful, because I find it rather difficult to swallow that when a Defence witness forgets an incident or forgets a fact they're just being untruthful, where if it's a positive thing for the Prosecution, well, then, they're just credible. So just please look at all of it. With respect to the prisoners, we also have the testimony of Mr. Zekic. I believe he said that there were 30 prisoners. Maybe Dusko Jevic came across other prisoners. We don't know. But the bottom line is you have the testimony. Please look it over carefully. I think Mr. Gavric came here and tried to be as truthful and honest as he possibly could, and that's exactly what he did, testified accordingly. I was hoping I wasn't going to have to speak about Mr. Nikolic, but I guess I'm -- I feel like -- like I have to. Was he a self-manager? Well, anybody who doesn't report for six days to his commander during the most important military campaign, I would say he's self-managing. Also, if you recall, when I showed him the document, the battle -- the combat order of July 5th, you recall how he was agitated that he had not been shown this document. You know, pouting like a little kid that he had been left out of the game and, therefore, he was going to take his toys and go home, which is basically what he did. He stayed in his office for those five or six days, whatever it was. But then, if you recall -- I'll slow down for the interpreters. I'm getting a little excited here. It's not good for my heart. But also you might recall where we went to that one part in the combat order with respect to the use of the military police, that they were going to be used as reserves. But remember, he said that this was an illegal and improper use of the military police. He was kind of vehement. And I touched on that with others including Mr. Keserovic who said that was fine. Mr. Obrenovic, he equivocated a little bit of course. You have to remember the Obrenovic was the Prosecution's witness at that point looking for a sweetheart of a deal. But there were other witnesses that said there was nothing wrong with using the military police for reserve, and Mr. McCloskey acknowledged that yesterday or the day before that they were used for combat purposes. But what was my point? My point was go back to the transcript. I urge you, I beg you, I plead with you that you will see where he says that had he known about this he would have reported him to Beara. So -- and you have to keep in mind. Here is the guy -- I am going to get a little excited now. Because of this self-management thing, you have to understand, Your Honours that this was a captain, not even first class reserve officer, but he was security, and this captain had the right to arrest his commander, but his commander did not have the right to have him arrested. There -- because he was security. It's a little bit like the gestapo. They're in a different category. They have their own sets of rules, and they have different powers, and they can do those sorts of things. He had his own car. He didn't have to sign in when he went into the headquarters. He came and went as he pleased. So was he a self-manager? I dare say so he was. I could go on and on about him, but I -- well, let me just touch on one other point which goes back to (redacted) testimony. Who was he coordinating? He was probably coordinating the military police that were there, stand over here, stand over there. Where was there -- is there one witness, one credible witness who says that he was given an order by Momir Nikolic? One officer? Nobody came. And whose burden is it to prove that? It's not mine. They could have brought some people over. They brought one person, van Duijn, who said that he saw from the hand motions that he was a coordinator. Well, okay. Fine. I'm going to move on because I could go on for hours on Mr. Nikolic. The Jankovic report, the night of the 13th going into the 14th, there's some room for interpretation. I agree with the Prosecutor. That's what I call a reasonable, plausible explanation. That's why I find it rather difficult that when they see something like that they automatically dismiss it. They give it what we call the bum's rush. They don't have any time for it. And what I'm suggesting is look at it all. Consider the other plausible, reasonable explanations. And I think when you look at that, factor also Major Franken's comment when he comes up and he says, "I have the list of the people," and his response is, "Yeah, so what? We've captured 6.000 others." And I think, if I interpret that, is here is a man who has nothing to hide. It's like, yeah, so what you took the names. Well, I'm taking an accounting over here. Big deal. Nothing is going to happen to these people. So you have to factor all of that in. You know, the a-la-carte approach doesn't work. It helps them but it doesn't work. All right. We talked about reporting it, and maybe again - because I was trying to cover so much - as I indicated four and a half hours it's like giving Fidel Castro, you know, tell him to talk about the revolution in four and a half hours. It's impossible. I needed three or four days for my closing in all seriousness and I could have been methodical and not repetitive perhaps, but I had to hit a lot of points. But here is what I was trying to convey yesterday: That with respect to these activities, these atrocities, nobody is reporting to Colonel Blagojevic. He is going out in the field, and he's getting reports from his battalion commanders because that's what he is concerned with. There was no suggestion that Mr. Zekic or others weren't reporting to him. That's ludicrous. With respect to Mr. Trisic, first he was a Prosecution witness on the list. They didn't bring him. And I think that to me tells me a little bit. Why? There's the a-la-carte approach again. You never know what that dish may serve. So when we bring him here, look at everything in context. At one point when he's questioned by Manning or whoever it was, he also had indicated that he remembers seeing Mr. Blagojevic in Potocari, and that -- he recognised that that was a mistake. And everybody, everybody, and I think that Mr. McCloskey probably will probably agree with you - it's one of the few times - that there is absolutely no evidence that Mr. Blagojevic was in Potocari on the 12th. So why did Major Trisic say it? Was he trying to curry favour with Dean Manning at the time? Was he trying to entrap or to implicate Colonel Blagojevic? Could it be that he just missed -- was -- misspoke or just thought he saw him but didn't see him, expected to see him there so he just made an assumption? All of that is a possibility. Just like it's a possibility that he might have informed him and a possibility that he didn't inform him because he's getting some normal functional relationship orders that are not out of the ordinary, perfectly normal within the circumstances, and so -- and then again -- I got to -- I got to comment about this. Last week or whatever, the Prosecution wanted to introduce this witness that had been certified. Fair enough. And I objected to it. It comes in. And it comes in with the understanding that after all those years, witnesses may not totally recall everything, may not have an absolute independent recollection, but nonetheless the Court is going to take that into consideration among with other things. Well, can't we apply that principle to the Defence witnesses or does that only work for the Prosecution? Of course it works for our witnesses. Isn't it possible that after all those years that your memory gets clouded, you know, confused a little bit, especially the way memories work? You recall something, there are some gaps, you hear other things, you learn other things, they fill in the gaps and somehow the memory gets mixed up a little bit. So I think if you look at -- you have to look at his entire testimony. And I thought he was a very credible witness, and so I suggest that you look at his entire testimony. Now, with respect to P110, I did indicate yesterday, and I think here again -- I think if Mr. McCloskey wanted to be fair to me he should have said well, he did mention that there was one person at least that said about the 12th. Because I said that yesterday. I never said there was absolutely no witness that said anything about the 12th in Bratunac. I just didn't recall the number, but I knew that he had come in from the Krstic trial. He says in one of the buildings. Which buildings? Do we know that there was more than one building? Could it be that the gentleman was confused, that he got the 12th mixed up with the 13th? The Prosecution would have you believe, no, absolutely not. It's got to be the 12th. We suggest that the gentleman might be mistaken. It could have been the 13th. But he's only -- he's the only person that we have. And if this was so important, why do it through 92 bis? Why not bring him here and subject him to cross-examination if that was such a critical aspect, that all of these things were happening on the 12th versus the 13th? And I think that you need to consider as well. Now, with respect to Mr. Keserovic. With respect to Mr. Keserovic, you have to look at the entire testimony, and I just -- I don't want to go in and take up too much time. There's a whole page I could read, but I won't. I will just ask you to when you look at the Prosecutor's trial brief with respect to paragraph 307 and onwards, just kindly look at Mr. Keserovic's testimony on page 10641. There's a question where I talk about the use of the military police, and it goes down and I talk about the security organ. But I'll just read the last few lines starting with line 18. He says: "In practical terms, this means that any deployment or use of military police units is ordered and commanded by the commander of that unit. As for specific tasks throughout the military police services, the security organ has the authority to issue a task and assignment to a section, department, or whatever the military police has so that these tasks are then carried out by these individual services regardless," I underscore that, "regardless of the commander. But they could and should inform the commander about the results of those activities depending on the case or mission at hand." That's at page 10641. Again, we're not trying to shy away from the evidence. We're asking you not to look at them a la carte, that's all. And I would have preferred to have served you with a five- or seven-course meal. Instead we skipped the entrees and the dessert, and I was only able to give you a little snippet of my closing. In any event, getting back, just that one last point, and I'll now sit down. With respect to the testimony regarding the 12th, again the Prosecution in their brief it would be found on paragraph 257, again I don't want to go into it, but I think I would urge the Court to look at the various pages in the transcript. One would be page 1277, would be line 16 and 17; and then again on page 6741 to 6746. There was a question posed by Mr. Stojanovic to Witness 130, and I think you need to look at it all in context. And it is our firm belief that there's another reasonable and plausible explanation, and that is that the folks begin arriving in Orahovac on the afternoon of -- of the 14th and not on the night of the 13th, as suggested. I don't want to take up a lot of your time. I could read it and go over it, but I don't think that's the purpose of this rejoinder, which incidentally is quite enjoyable to do and quite useful. Since I won't get another opportunity to speak, I just want to say again, again that I am -- it has been an honour to have appeared before you, and I consider it a privilege, actually, to have represented Colonel Blagojevic. I want to thank everybody, the booths, technical, interpreters. I know they've had a tough time because I speak fast and maybe use some language that they're not familiar with in court. Ms. Katherine Gallagher has been extremely helpful. Mr. Ram Doraiswamy has been tremendous, and we should all be proud of him. And I want to thank my team. I want to thank Mr. Momirov over here who has been our case manager, and I have had the best co-counsel, Ms. Tomanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just a few sentences. If I understood Mr. McCloskey correctly, he agrees that there is not sufficient evidence for paragraph 46.4, the Kravica warehouse, and he does not charge Dragan Jokic as a member of the joint criminal enterprise for opportunistic killings in the Bratunac Brigade. This would be in with 98 bis, 47.1, 47.3, 47.4, paragraphs of the amended joinder indictment, that is. That is what I'm referring to. I hope that I did not receive a mistranslation or something. I hope that this is actually what has been said. As for the arguments presented during the rebuttal, there was a thesis that Jokic knew about the prisoners in Petkovci, Rocevic, Orahovac, and Kula, and there was then our thesis that that does not mean that he knew of the fate of these prisoners. It is for you, Your Honours, to assess the facts. Is this sufficient evidence to prove that this person knew of the fate of these prisoners? The Prosecutor says in his rebuttal that these schools were not detention centres. That is correct. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is not a single place or a prison for such a large number of prisoners. Your Honours, you had the opportunity to see the site itself of the prison of the Zvornik Brigade. It was quite literally one room. So if the prisoners are kept in schools, does that mean that a person can infer that they would be executed? I think that this is a conclusion that is pretentious. That is the opinion of this Defence. The Prosecutor says that in the notebook of the duty operations officer for the 16th of July there is a note made again by Witness P130, who testifies about this, that the request for machinery and trucks from the 1st Infantry Battalion was conveyed to Jokic and Milosevic. I kindly ask you, Your Honours, that when assessing this evidence you look at this same exhibit and also the note relating to the morning of the 17th. And this same person, P130, notes that the 1st Battalion asks what was going on with this machinery and this truck, which clearly indicates that the machine and the truck did not arrive in the morning of the 17th. How did he convey this to Jokic? How can Jokic direct the burial operation in Branjevo on the 17th, therefore? Again, Your Honours, it is up to you to decide. And finally, in his rebuttal today, the Prosecutor said Jokic, on the 16th of July, sent an excavator to Kozluk. He had reason to know why that excavator was going there. Your Honours, I tried to speak about the statement made by Witness Mitrovic Milos as much as briefly possible. He spoke about this, and you will recall that he took the skip torpedo machine there which has a very small bucket. Therefore, its capacity is very limited. So he could not carry out the assignment given to him by his platoon commander, not Dragan Jokic. And this same Prosecution witness says that after an hour, because he could not do this, the ULT220 came and finished the job. So what would be the answer? If Dragan Jokic knows why the machine was supposed to go there to Kozluk, and if Dragan Jokic knows what the characteristics of these machines are, and he does know because he is an engineer, why is he sending the wrong machine then? Why is he then sending a machine that cannot do what was required and what Dragan Jokic was supposed to know about? The Defence reiterates it was actually the other way around. This is proof that at that moment, he did not know why the skip torpedo went there. At that moment in Kozluk, he could have been doing thousands of things. Or, rather, the skip-torpedo could have done so many different things that it was capable of performing. At any rate, Your Honours, all of this shows the degree of difficulty of the job before us. I do not wish to be pathetic in any way. You will weigh all the evidence, everything that all of us said in this courtroom. And first and foremost, you will assess what the truth is and thus reach a conclusion about everything that had happened. Allow me, in closing, to thank you all. This was an experience of a lifetime, as far as I'm concerned. I will probably never again have this kind of experience. And I hope I did not hurt anybody as I did this job, and I hope that I did not cause anyone any pain as I performed my duties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to mention at this stage? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last housekeeping matter for the record that we all -- counsel had talked briefly about because there's been kind of an odd situation with -- with P130, and we wanted to get on the record something more official about him, because we know about the various motions and all, and I know that was a difficult issue for the Court, but I think in putting our heads together, we came up with -- and this was done very -- very briefly so I'll need some help. Instead of just kind of leaving that motion out there as not part of the record, if we could agree to something to the effect that P130, if called to testify, would say that he did not testify fully and completely at the time he testified here and that he in fact testified falsely at places. This was the foundation of the motion. This is something that's been in the air. I don't know how else to deal with this issue, Your Honour, but I think we should get it on the record in a simple way like that so it's not sitting in the background. The -- and I go back to my culture. We have all the statements, but I would never put those statements to the trier of fact because of the detail that was in them until the Judges allowed us to. So that's why you didn't get them, but -- and I think that's probably the way counsel would have had it as well since we come from that same culture. So I apologise for the awkwardness of that situation, but I think for the record, we have to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, Mr. McCloskey did come up to me and he did mention 130, and my respond was oh, the perjurer. That's how I characterise him. Because somebody who comes to court, takes an oath to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth -- see, that whole truth, that's what gets you into trouble sometimes. That's why Ms. Celanovic was having a hard time as a lawyer answering those questions. But that's the only way to characterise this guy. So if we need to condense it and give it the Reader's Digest version, as I would say, we just say 130 committed perjury. Full stop, end of story. There's nothing more to say. I don't think that we should -- and I would love to see -- I would love to see something from the Prosecution charging with perjury, because I think that's what we need to do. This is a serious court. These are serious matters. And if somebody has come in and has committed perjury, he should be punished. That's the end of the story. So I'm afraid I cannot be generous with this fellow. But he's a perjurer and he committed perjury, so we should just say P130 committed perjury, full stop, and I'll be happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we also believe that no court ruling can be based on this witness's testimony. The system that I come from would qualify the testimony of this witness as perjury or false testimony. Should the judgement be based on the testimony of this kind of witness, then there should be a retrial. That would be the only legal remedy. I think that this is sufficient for us. We shall only say that we cannot accept the testimony of this witness, and his testimony has no weight for us whatsoever. May I be allowed to remind you, during my work in the field for these three years, having heard the story of Witness P130 and having asked him myself whether he had been to Petkovci, to Branjevo or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... It is a legal concern that I have for the record that this has all been out, but I think we're all in close enough agreement that there is a problem with P130's testimony. All I want to do is acknowledge that that is part of the record, that he did not tell the whole truth, that he has admitted that he testified falsely, and so that you can consider that, because without that there may be an allegation that you would have considered that and it wasn't on the record, thereby your judgement could be flawed. I don't -- I hope that won't happen, but as we know, we don't know what's going to happen in the Appeals Chamber. So given the importance of the topic and we're so close on all this, that's what I think solves the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that during these procedures, each party has the right to offer their assessment of the testimony of one witness and the views from both parties has already been in the transcript. We will take note of that. But don't forget the Bench will read his testimony and arrive at our own conclusions concerning with his testimony. It is so decided. Well, it seems to me that we are approaching to the end of these proceedings of this case. The hearing of this case began on May 14, 2003. Before and during the proceedings, two other co-accused, Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic, pleaded guilty, and the Chamber entered convictions for them accordingly. Also, the Judges and the counsel from both parties made a field trip to certain of the locations mentioned in the indictment. According to Mr. Stojanovic, we sat in this courtroom for 145 trial days, not including the days for motion hearings, Status Conferences, opening and closing statements. We entertained about 135 witnesses called by both parties, including both live and 92 and 94 witnesses. The Chamber admitted over 1.000 documents into the evidence. Since the hearing of this case has come to its end, on behalf of Judge Vassylenko and Judge Argibay, I would like to thank both parties for their hard work, the devotion, and kind cooperation in assisting the Bench to find the truth in this case. We believe that during the proceedings both parties demonstrated great professionalism, diligence, and a profound understanding of the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Bench benefited a lot from the presentations of both parties in the past 16 months. The Bench would also like to express our sincere thanks to all those who contribute to this case, the Court Deputy, court reporter, usher, interpreters, and the translators, technicians, as well as the security guards. Without any of them, we just could not keep the proceedings going for a single day. Finally, please allow me to quote what Mr. McCloskey said in his last sentence in his closing argument. He said, "It is with great honour, respect, and confidence that we pass the case that we have cradled for eight years on to you for your final judgement." We have a feeling that the burden has been shifted on our shoulders. The Chamber will withdraw and deliberate in a private room from now on, and the judgement is expected to be delivered at the end of this year or at the early beginning of next year. Ladies and gentlemen, in accordance with the Rule 87 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, as the Presiding Judge of this case I declare the hearing of this case is closed. The hearing is adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.24 p.m.
